title: Not so Fast: Revised Calibration of SIDM Core Collapse

paper.title: Not so Fast: Revised Calibration of SIDM Core Collapse
paper.abstract: Abstract Self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) haloes undergo gravothermal evolution whose late-time behaviour is central to predictions for dense substructure and black-hole seed formation. We revisit the calibration of this evolution using a new spherical Direct Simulation Monte Carlo code, SphDSMC , which follows spherically symmetric SIDM systems without force softening and to substantially higher central densities than standard N N -body simulations. We compare SphDSMC calculations with conventional N N -body simulations and with one-dimensional gravothermal fluid models. We show that N N -body results converge to SphDSMC only for softening lengths significantly smaller than those normally adopted for collisionless simulations, and that allowing multiple scatterings per particle per time step does not introduce significant errors when implemented appropriately. Calibrating the gravothermal fluid equations against SphDSMC , we find that the commonly used harmonic interpolation between the long- and short-mean-free-path conductivities is inaccurate. A gentler transition, however, yields excellent agreement for NFW haloes over a range of concentrations and truncation radii, with a single long-mean-free-path conductivity parameter. The revised calibration gives a long-mean-free-path collapse time that is somewhat shorter than previous estimates, but we show that collapse slows dramatically once the core becomes optically thick. We provide fitting functions for the late-time evolution and argue that black-hole seed formation by SIDM gravothermal collapse has generally been underestimated in duration, making it unlikely to explain the massive high-redshift black holes inferred from JWST observations without additional physics.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) remains one of the most widely studied alternatives to collisionless cold dark matter (CDM). In SIDM models, dark-matter particles undergo non-gravitational scattering, allowing heat and momentum transport within haloes while preserving the large-scale phenomenology of Λ \Lambda CDM ( Spergel and Steinhardt, 2000 ; Tulin and Yu, 2018 ; Adhikari et al., 2025 ) . Self-scattering initially transports heat from the hotter outer halo into the colder inner region, driving the formation of an approximately isothermal core and reducing the central density. At later times, the direction of net heat flow reverses and the system enters a gravothermal-collapse phase, during which the central region contracts, heats up and becomes denser ( Lynden-Bell and Wood, 1968 ; Balberg et al., 2002 ; Koda and Shapiro, 2011 ; Outmezguine et al., 2023 ) . This behaviour is closely related to the gravothermal catastrophe long studied in collisional stellar systems. Gravothermal collapse has attracted increasing attention because it provides a natural mechanism for generating substantial halo-to-halo diversity. Haloes with similar virial masses but different concentrations, accretion histories or tidal environments need not be observed in the same thermodynamic state: some may still be in the core-expansion phase, while others may already have collapsed to much higher central densities. This offers a plausible route to understanding the observed diversity of rotation curves, including the coexistence of diffuse and comparatively dense systems within the same broad mass range ( Ren et al., 2019 ; Sameie et al., 2020 ; Nadler et al., 2023 ; Roberts et al., 2025b ; Fischer and Yu, 2026 ) . Related considerations arise in the context of strong gravitational lensing. Observational studies have pointed to unexpectedly dense perturbers ( Minor et al., 2021 ) and to an excess of galaxy-galaxy strong lensing in clusters relative to standard theoretical expectations ( Meneghetti et al., 2023 ; Natarajan et al., 2026 ) . SIDM subhaloes that have undergone gravothermal collapse provide a natural source of compact, high-density structures capable of enhancing such signals, particularly when tidal effects accelerate their evolution after infall ( Nishikawa et al., 2020 ; Gilman et al., 2021 ; Zeng et al., 2022 ; Shah and Adhikari, 2024 ; Dutra et al., 2025 ) . Perhaps the most far-reaching implication of SIDM gravothermal collapse is that sufficiently deep collapse can trigger black hole (BH) formation. In particular, if the self-interactions of the dark matter particles do not allow the formation of any bound states, the runaway gravothermal collapse will drive the core to relativistic velocities at which point the core undergoes catastrophic collapse into a BH via the radial instability ( Zel’dovich and Podurets, 1966 ; Shapiro and Teukolsky, 1985 ; Balberg and Shapiro, 2002 ) . More recent studies have revived this idea in several contexts, including intermediate-mass BH formation in Milky Way satellites ( Meshveliani et al., 2023 ) , and BH seeding in high-redshift haloes which might help to explain the unexpectedly early appearance of massive accreting BHs in the Universe ( Pollack et al., 2015 ; Choquette et al., 2019 ; Feng et al., 2021 ; Feng et al., 2022 ) . This connection has become especially timely in light of the discovery by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) of the “little red dots” (LRDs): a numerous population of compact, red, broad-line sources at high redshift that appear consistent with rapidly growing black holes embedded in dense gaseous environments ( Kocevski et al., 2023 ; Greene et al., 2024 ; Matthee et al., 2024 ) . Several recent works have therefore proposed SIDM core collapse as a viable channel for producing the heavy black-hole seeds needed for LRDs ( Feng et al., 2025 ; Roberts et al., 2026 ; Shen et al., 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ) . In each of these applications, the relevant phenomenology depends sensitively on the gravothermal-collapse time. Whether one is interested in the diversity of dwarf-galaxy rotation curves, the existence of dense strong-lensing perturbers, or the formation of early black-hole seeds, the viability of the SIDM interpretation depends on whether collapse can occur within the available cosmic time. In practice, collapse times are inferred using two main approaches: particle-based N N -body simulations with stochastic scattering and one-dimensional (1D) gravothermal fluid (GTF) calculations. These methods are complementary, but they rely on different assumptions and each has its own shortcomings. The gravothermal fluid approach, introduced for SIDM haloes by Balberg et al. (2002) and developed further in many later studies ( Ahn and Shapiro, 2005 ; Koda and Shapiro, 2011 ; Pollack et al., 2015 ; Essig et al., 2019 ; Nishikawa et al., 2020 ; Outmezguine et al., 2023 ) , assumes a spherical, non-rotating halo evolving quasi-statically through a sequence of hydrostatic states. Its main advantage is that it is inexpensive and can follow the system over a large dynamic range, making it well suited for mapping collapse times across parameter space. The key limitation, however, is that one of the main ingredients, the effective conductivity in the long-mean-free path (LMFP) regime, is not know from first principles. Instead, it is typically parameterised by a single free parameter which is calibrated against the results from N N -body simulations. In addition, one generally interpolates between the long and short-mean-free part (SMFP) regimes using an ad-hoc interpolation scheme that has not been adequately tested. The alternative route is direct N N -body simulation, in which SIDM scattering is implemented probabilistically between neighbouring particles on top of the collisionless gravitational evolution ( Burkert, 2000 ; Kochanek and White, 2000 ; Yoshida et al., 2000 ; Davé et al., 2001 ; Vogelsberger et al., 2012 ; Rocha et al., 2013 ) . The major advantage of this approach is that it does not impose spherical symmetry, hydrostatic equilibrium or isotropy, and can naturally capture mergers, cosmological accretion and tidal stripping ( Vogelsberger et al., 2012 ; Rocha et al., 2013 ; Zavala et al., 2013 ; Sameie et al., 2020 ; Turner et al., 2021 ; Zeng et al., 2022 ) . This is relevant because the collapse time can be strongly altered by the environment: tidal stripping tends to accelerate collapse by steepening the outer density profile and enhancing the outward heat flux ( Nishikawa et al., 2020 ; Sameie et al., 2020 ; Zeng et al., 2022 ; Shah and Adhikari, 2024 ) , while continued accretion, mergers or other heating processes can delay or interrupt collapse ( Ahn and Shapiro, 2005 ; Turner et al., 2021 ; Outmezguine et al., 2023 ; Silverman et al., 2026 ) . On the other hand, properly resolving the gravothermal collapse is numerically challenging. As the core contracts, the central density rises rapidly, local scattering and dynamical time-scales become very short, and the inferred collapse time becomes sensitive to particle number, force softening, time integration, and the details of the scattering implementation ( Meskhidze et al., 2022 ; Palubski et al., 2024 ; Fischer et al., 2024 ; Fischer et al., 2025 ; Mace et al., 2024 ) . Recent numerical studies have shown that these effects can shift the collapse time appreciably, so even the simulation-based estimates are not yet fully settled. This in turn impacts the calibration of the LMFP conductivity used in the GTF codes, and thus the collapse times that these codes predict. In this work we study the gravothermal core collapse of SIDM haloes using a two-step approach. We first present a new simulation code, similar in spirit to the kinetic solver KiSS-SIDM recently developed by Gurian and May (2025) and to the NSphere code developed independently by Kamionkowski and Sigurdson (2026) . This code has several advantages over standard N N -body codes. Here, we use it to calibrate the conductivity used in GTF codes. We show that the harmonic form that has hitherto been used to interpolate the conductivity parameter between the long- and short-mean-free paths is inaccurate. We propose an alternative form and show that a single value for the conductivity parameter in the LMFP regime suffices to model the gravothermal evolution of any NFW halo, independent of its concentration parameter or the level to which it has been truncated. This paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the various numerical methods used here to study the gravothermal evolution of SIDM haloes, including a detailed description of the haloes used throughout. Section 3 starts with a validation of our new SphDSMC code against N N -body simulations, followed by an improved calibration of the conductivity used in the gravothermal fluid equations and a discussion of outstanding issues. In Section 4 we present a detailed discussion of the core collapse time of NFW haloes and present a fitting function that accurately captures the late stages of their gravothermal collapse. This is used in Section 4.1 to demonstrate that the time-scale on which core collapse can produce a seed black hole mass is orders of magnitude larger than previously assumed. We summarize our findings in Section 5 . Finally, Appendix A describes the Monte-Carlo method used in our N N -body simulations, including a detailed demonstration that, contrary to claims in the literature, it is justified to allow multiple scatter events per particle per time. Appendix B discusses the impact of stochasticity due to realisation noise on the ability to determine the core collapse time of an SIDM halo, and Appendix C presents a validation of the new SphDSMC code. Throughout, we assume a flat Λ \Lambda CDM cosmology with Ω m = 0.3 \Omega_{\rm m}=0.3 and H 0 = 70 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=70\>{\rm km}\,{\rm s}^{-1}\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1} , unless stated otherwise.

sections.heading: 2 Methodology
sections.text: The main goal of this paper is to use simulations of SIDM haloes undergoing core collapse to calibrate the conductivity used in gravothermal fluid (hereafter GTF ) codes to model the same process. For the simulations, we use a new spherical Direct Simulation Monte Carlo code developed by the authors, called SphDSMC , which is similar to, but independent of, two separate codes recently developed by Gurian and May (2025) and by Kamionkowski and Sigurdson (2026) and Kamionkowski et al. (2026) , respectively. SphDSMC assumes spherical symmetry and integrates the radial coordinates of particles in an N N -body system following the approach pioneered by Hénon and Spitzer more than half a century ago ( Hénon, 1964 ; Hénon, 1971 ; Spitzer and Hart, 1971 ) , while treating the collisional scattering using the Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method ( Bird, 1994 ) . The main advantages of this method are that it (i) is much faster than the N N -body method, (ii) can integrate the system down to much higher core densities, (iii) does not require any particle softening, and (iv) typically results in much better energy conservation than standard N N -body codes. The downside is that it only works for spherically symmetric systems. As already advocated by Gurian and May (2025) and Kamionkowski et al. (2026) this method is ideally suited for studying the core collapse of (spherical) SIDM haloes. The GTF method solves the evolution of a spherical SIDM halo on a 1D radial grid treating the system as a gravothermal fluid following Lynden-Bell and Eggleton (1980) and Balberg et al. (2002) . The main advantages of this method are that it is even faster than the SphDSMC method, and that it is not subject to realisation noise; as input it takes a discretised version of the smooth density and velocity dispersion profiles of the system in question, rather than the phase-space coordinates of a discrete set of points sampled from the system’s distribution function. As shown in Appendix B , suppressing the realisation noise sufficiently for a reliable measure of the core collapse time-scale, N N -body and SphDSMC simulations typically require at least 10 6 10^{6} particles per halo ( Mace et al., 2024 , see also) . As a consequence, it typically takes several hours to simulate the core collapse of a single halo with the SphDSMC code, and 5-10 times longer with a standard N N -body code. The GTF code, on the other hand, typically already yields converged results for a radial grid consisting of only a few hundred bins and it only takes a few seconds to run it to central densities comparable to what can be achieved with SphDSMC or N N -body simulations. The main downside of the GTF method is that it has a free parameter that characterises the conductivity in the LMFP regime. This parameter directly impacts the time-scale on which the system undergoes core collapse but has thus far eluded a derivation from first principles. Hence, it is common to calibrate this parameter against N N -body simulations. However, since the latter are subject to significant uncertainties and systematics (see Palubski et al., 2024 ; Fischer et al., 2024 ; Mace et al., 2024 , and Section 3.1 ) , this gives rise to a catch-22 situation. Indeed, different studies have inferred calibration constants that differ by more than 25% and it is currently unclear whether this reflects inconsistencies among the N N -body simulations or whether the calibration parameter itself varies with properties of the halo in question. The goal of this paper is to avoid these issues by calibrating the GTF method against results of the SphDSMC method. As we will show, part of the issue is that the ad-hoc interpolation scheme that has been used to link the short- and long-mean-free path regimes is inaccurate. sections.heading: 2.2 The Spherical Direct Simulation Monte Carlo Code
sections.text: The SphDSMC code is based on methods devised in the 1960s and early 70s by Hénon and Spitzer ( Hénon, 1964 ; Hénon, 1971 ; Spitzer and Hart, 1971 , e.g.,) mainly to model the dynamical evolution of spherical star clusters. These methods explicitly assume spherical symmetry throughout the entire evolution of the system, which allows a drastic speed up of the orbit integration compared to standard N N -body codes. This method was recently revived and adapted to modelling SIDM haloes in Gurian and May (2025) and independently in a recent series of papers by M. Kamionkowski and K. Sigurdson ( Kamionkowski and Sigurdson, 2026 ; Kamionkowski et al., 2026 ; Kamionkowski and Sigurdson, 2025 ) . We have developed a similar code that uses elements from all these previous studies, as described below. SphDSMC takes as input the same initial condition data as standard N N -body simulations, i.e., the initial Cartesian positions and velocities of the N p N_{\rm p} particles that make up the (spherical) system. Each time step, SphDSMC first sorts the particles in the order of increasing distance r i r_{i} from the centre, where i = 1 , 2 , … , N p i=1,2,...,N_{\rm p} . Since typically only a few particles change their rank order per time step, we use a standard insertion sort algorithm, which achieves close-to 𝒪 ⁡ ( N p ) {\cal O}(N_{\rm p}) performance for nearly-sorted data. Next, it uses a standard kick-drift-kick leapfrog integration scheme to advance the particles a time step Δ ​ t \Delta t solving the radial equations of motion given by d ​ r i d ​ t \displaystyle{{\rm d}r_{i}\over{\rm d}t} = \displaystyle= v r , i , \displaystyle v_{r,i}\,, d ​ v r , i d ​ t \displaystyle{{\rm d}v_{{\rm r},i}\over{\rm d}t} = \displaystyle= − G ⁡ ( i − 1 2 ) ​ m p r i 2 + l i 2 r i 3 . \displaystyle-{G\,(i-\frac{1}{2})\,m_{\rm p}\over r^{2}_{i}}+{l_{i}^{2}\over r_{i}^{3}}\,. Following Kamionkowski and Sigurdson (2026) we use Levi-Civita (LC) regularization ( Levi-Civita, 1920 ) to circumvent these problems, albeit using a somewhat different implementation. sections.heading: 2.2.1 Spatial and temporal resolution
sections.text: Similarly to N N -body simulations, SphDSMC simulations are limited by finite spatial and temporal resolution. The finite spatial resolution mainly manifests as an inability to resolve the ever-shrinking mean-free-path of the particles during core collapse. As indicated above, we refine the radial shells in an attempt to ensure that Δ ​ r < λ mfp \Delta r<\lambda_{\rm mfp} , but we only split the shells if they have a minimum of N shell = 32 N_{\rm shell}=32 particles. Each halo will, at some point during its core collapse, reach a point when the central region can no longer be refined because of this constraint. We define r fail r_{\rm fail} as the radius within which the refinement criterion can no longer be satisfied. In principle, for r < r fail r<r_{\rm fail} the system experiences too much transport due to the fact that the simulation fails to resolve the mean-free-path. However, as long as r fail r_{\rm fail} is small compared to the system’s core radius this enhanced transport will have little net effect since there are no significant density or temperature gradients within the core. In practice, as detailed in Section 3.3 , we find that when r fail r_{\rm fail} exceeds the core radius the results start to reveal weak signs of accelerated core collapse compared to the gravothermal fluid simulations due to this artificially enhanced transport. The finite temporal resolution mainly comes at play for large collision cross sections. As is evident from equations ( 12 )-( 13 ), the ratio Δ ​ t coll / Δ ​ t grav ∝ Kn \Delta t_{\rm coll}/\Delta t_{\rm grav}\propto{\rm Kn} . During core collapse, the Knudsen number of the core continues to decrease. Hence, at some point the time stepping of the simulations is controlled by the collision time rather than the dynamical time, and this transition occurs earlier for larger σ m \sigma_{\rm m} . During core collapse Δ ​ t coll \Delta t_{\rm coll} rapidly decreases with time, and at some point the simulations have to be terminated because progress becomes too slow and computationally expensive. In principle, the simulations can be greatly sped up using larger values of ζ \zeta . We have experimented using values for ζ \zeta as large as 100 100 , and find that this has a negligible impact on the results; the system’s evolution is virtually indistinguishable from that obtained using ζ = 1 \zeta=1 . At first sight this seems surprising, since using a time step Δ ​ t ≫ t coll \Delta t\gg t_{\rm coll} implies that the particles can ‘free-stream’ too large a distance in between collisions, thus once more causing transport that is too efficient. Note, though, that t coll t_{\rm coll} is defined as the minimum collision time, which typically occurs at the centre of the core. Outside of the core, both ρ \rho and v max v_{\rm max} decline rapidly, so that most of the illicit free streaming is confined to the isothermal core, where the net transport is negligible. We suspect that this explains why large values of ζ \zeta do not seem to have significant adverse effects, but we leave a more detailed investigation for future work. In what follows, we take the conservative approach, and adopt ζ = 1 \zeta=1 throughout.

sections.heading: 2.3 Gravothermal Fluid Code
sections.text: We compare the results of our SphDSMC code to those obtained with a gravothermal fluid ( GTF ) code, which treats the SIDM halo as a conducting gravothermal fluid that can be treated as a mono-atomic ideal gas. Originally developed by Lynden-Bell and Eggleton (1980) to model the collisional evolution of globular clusters, it has since been used by numerous authors to model the evolution of SIDM haloes ( Balberg et al., 2002 ; Koda and Shapiro, 2011 ; Pollack et al., 2015 ; Essig et al., 2019 ; Nishikawa et al., 2020 , e.g.,) . The GTF method solves the gravothermal fluid equations on a 1D radial grid, and thus also assumes spherical symmetry. Consider a spherical SIDM halo with a density profile ρ ⁡ ( r , t ) \rho(r,t) and an enclosed mass M ⁡ ( r , t ) M(r,t) at radius r r and time t t . Assume the halo to be isotropic and in quasi-static virial equilibrium with a 1D velocity dispersion v ⁡ ( r , t ) v(r,t) . Due to self-interactions, characterised by a cross section per unit mass σ m \sigma_{\rm m} , heat flows in the radial direction with a luminosity L ⁡ ( r , t ) L(r,t) through a spherical shell at radius r r . The corresponding heat flux obeys Fourier’s law of thermal conduction, L 4 ​ π ​ r 2 = − κ ​ ∂ T ∂ r , \frac{L}{4\pi r^{2}}=-\kappa\frac{\partial T}{\partial r}\,, (14) with κ \kappa the conductivity and k B ​ T = m ​ v 2 k_{\rm B}T=mv^{2} a measure of the temperature of the particles of mass m m . In addition to the heat conduction equation, the gravothermal fluid also obeys mass conservation, ∂ M ∂ r = 4 ​ π ​ r 2 ​ ρ , \frac{\partial M}{\partial r}=4\pi r^{2}\rho\,, (15) hydrostatic equilibrium, ∂ ρ ​ v 2 ∂ r = − G ​ M ​ ρ r 2 , \frac{\partial\rho v^{2}}{\partial r}=-\frac{GM\rho}{r^{2}}\,, (16) where we have defined the pressure P = ρ ​ v 2 P=\rho v^{2} , and the first law of thermodynamics which can be written as ∂ L ∂ r = − 4 ​ π ​ ρ ​ r 2 ​ v 2 ​ ( ∂ ∂ t ) M ​ ln ⁡ ( v 3 / ρ ) , \frac{\partial L}{\partial r}=-4\pi\rho r^{2}v^{2}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\right)_{M}\ln(v^{3}/\rho)\,, (17) with s = ln ⁡ ( v 3 / ρ ) s=\ln(v^{3}/\rho) an effective entropy. Strictly speaking, Fourier’s law of thermal conduction is valid in the SMFP regime, where Kn ≪ 1 {\rm Kn}\ll 1 . In this regime, Chapman-Enskog theory ( Lifshitz and Pitaevskii, 1981 ) dictates that the conductivity is given by κ SMFP = 3 2 ​ b a ​ n ​ k B ​ λ mfp 2 t r = 3 2 ​ b ​ k B m ​ v σ m , \kappa_{\rm SMFP}=\frac{3}{2}{b\over a}\,n\,k_{\rm B}{\lambda_{\rm mfp}^{2}\over t_{\rm r}}=\frac{3}{2}\,b\,{k_{\rm B}\over m}\,{v\over\sigma_{\rm m}}\,, (18) ( Balberg et al., 2002 ; Koda and Shapiro, 2011 ) , where n = ρ / m n=\rho/m is the number density of particles, b = 25 ​ π / 32 b=25\sqrt{\pi}/32 is the effective impact parameter and t r ≡ λ mfp / ( a ​ v ) t_{\rm r}\equiv\lambda_{\rm mfp}/(av) is the local collision time with a = 4 / π a=4/\sqrt{\pi} a coefficient relevant for hard-sphere scattering of particles with a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution ( Reif, 1965 ) . In the LMFP regime no formal expression for the conductivity exists, but Lynden-Bell and Eggleton (1980) have shown that an empirical relation of the form κ LMFP = 3 2 ​ β ​ n ​ k B ​ H 2 t r = 3 2 ​ β π 3 / 2 ​ k B m ​ ρ ​ v 3 ​ σ m G , \kappa_{\rm LMFP}=\frac{3}{2}\beta\,n\,k_{\rm B}{H^{2}\over t_{\rm r}}=\frac{3}{2}\,{\beta\over\pi^{3/2}}\,{k_{\rm B}\over m}\,{\rho v^{3}\sigma_{\rm m}\over G}\,, (19) with β \beta a free calibration parameter of order unity (see below), can adequately describe the gravothermal collapse of globular clusters. In order to interpolate between these two regimes, Balberg et al. (2002) adopted the harmonic form κ = [ κ SMFP − 1 + κ LMFP − 1 ] − 1 \kappa=\left[\kappa_{\rm SMFP}^{-1}+\kappa_{\rm LMFP}^{-1}\right]^{-1} (20) which has been used by all subsequent SIDM studies based on the gravothermal fluid equations. Given appropriate boundary conditions, equations ( 14 )–( 17 ) may be solved from a set of initial radial profiles. We employ a Lagrangian scheme in which each time step consists of two stages: (1) a conduction step in which equations ( 14 ) and ( 17 ) are solved, and (2) a “revirialisation” step, in which hydrostatic equilibrium (equation [ 16 ]) is restored by adjusting the radii of the Lagrangian mass shells. During the conduction step, the specific energy u i = 3 ​ v i 2 / 2 u_{i}=3v^{2}_{i}/2 , of each cell i i is updated while the density profile is held fixed. We do so using an implicit scheme, for which u i ( n + 1 ) \displaystyle{u_{i}}^{(n+1)} = u i ( n ) + \displaystyle={u_{i}}^{(n)}+ (21) Δ ​ t ⋅ f ⁡ ( u i − 1 ( n + 1 ) , u i ( n + 1 ) , u i + 1 ( n + 1 ) , ρ i − 1 , ρ i , ρ i + 1 ) , \displaystyle\Delta t\cdot f\left(u_{i-1}^{(n+1)},u_{i}^{(n+1)},u_{i+1}^{(n+1)},\rho_{i-1},\rho_{i},\rho_{i+1}\right)\,, where the superscript denotes the time step and u i ( n + 1 ) = u i ( n ) + Δ ​ u i {u_{i}}^{(n+1)}={u_{i}}^{(n)}+\Delta u_{i} . Combining equations ( 14 ) and ( 17 ) in the quasi-static limit, we linearise for small changes in u u , and cast the update equations into a tridiagonal form in the variables { Δ ​ u i − 1 , Δ ​ u i , Δ ​ u i + 1 } \left\{\Delta u_{i-1},\Delta u_{i},\Delta u_{i+1}\right\} , which we solve using standard linear algebra routines. The conduction step pushes the system out of hydrostatic equilibrium, after which the system is revirialised by discretizing and linearising equation ( 16 ), recasting it into tridiagonal form, and solving for the radial displacements { Δ ​ r i − 1 , Δ ​ r i , Δ ​ r i + 1 } \left\{\Delta r_{i-1},\Delta r_{i},\Delta r_{i+1}\right\} . This revirialisation step is iterated until max i ⁡ | Δ ​ r i | / r i < 10 − 12 \max_{i}|\Delta r_{i}|/r_{i}<10^{-12} , which rarely requires more than three iterations. Finally, the density profile is updated according to equation ( 15 ). In order to ensure that the linear approximations used in the revirialisation step remain accurate, we adjust the time step such that the maximum fractional change in the specific energy remains sufficiently small, max i ⁡ ( | Δ ​ u i | u i ) < 10 − 4 \max_{i}\left({|\Delta u_{i}|\over u_{i}}\right)<10^{-4} (22) With these choices, our GTF implementation is both fast and stable, enabling typical systems to be evolved through central density increases in excess of 10 orders of magnitude in only a few minutes on a standard modern processor. We have verified that the resulting evolution accurately matches that obtained using more conservative time step criteria.

sections.heading: 2.5 Core Properties
sections.text: Throughout, we define the ‘core’ as the region inside the radius r c r_{\rm c} , defined according to ρ ⁡ ( r c ) = ρ 0 / 2 \rho(r_{\rm c})=\rho_{0}/2 . For the SphDSMC simulations, ρ 0 \rho_{0} is defined as the average density that encloses the innermost 250 particles. For the GTF code, it is defined as the density of the innermost radial bin. Although these definitions are not identical, in practice the core region is homogeneous enough that we can meaningfully compare these quantities. In addition to the core radius and core density, we also compute the core mass M c = M ( < r c ) M_{\rm c}=M(<r_{\rm c}) and the core’s velocity dispersion, v c v_{\rm c} . The latter is defined as the mass- or particle-weighted velocity dispersion inside r c r_{\rm c} . We have also experimented using an alternative definition of the core, for which the core radius is defined as the innermost radius where d ​ log ⁡ ρ / d ​ log ⁡ r = − 2 {\rm d}\log\rho/{\rm d}\log r=-2 . Although this yields values for the core properties that can be quite different during the early stage of core formation, once the system has reached the state in which the core size is largest and the gravothermal collapse kicks in, both core definitions yield comparable results, and none of the results presented here depend significantly on which of these two core definitions we adopt. For the SphDSMC simulations, all radial profiles and their (logarithmic) gradients are computed using Savitsky-Golay filtering ( Savitzky and Golay, 1964 ) to suppress the impact of discreteness noise. sections.heading: 3.1 Comparing SphDSMC to N N -body
sections.text: Before presenting a detailed comparison of the SphDSMC and GTF codes, we first compare some results of the SphDSMC code to those of a standard N N -body simulation. In particular, we use a modified version of the hierarchical N N -body treecode , written by J. Barnes but modified to account for self-interactions following the method described in detail in van den Bosch and Dattathri (2026) to which we refer the reader for more details. Briefly, the code uses a Barnes and Hut (1986) octree to compute accelerations based on a multipole expansion up to quadrupole order and a straightforward second order leap-frog integration scheme to solve the equations of motion. The forces between the particles are softened using a simple Plummer softening, and the opening angle for the tree structure is set to θ = 0.7 \theta=0.7 . The elastic and isotropic scattering of the particles is treated using a Monte Carlo method similar to that of Vogelsberger et al. (2012) . The main difference between our method and that of Vogelsberger et al. and all other methods that have been presented in the literature ( Kochanek and White, 2000 ; Koda and Shapiro, 2011 ; Rocha et al., 2013 ; Kim et al., 2017 ; Elbert et al., 2018 ; Fischer et al., 2025 , e.g.,) , is that we allow particles to undergo multiple scattering events per time step 4 4 4 While this paper was under review, two papers appeared ( Fischer et al., 2026 ; Zier et al., 2026 ) introducing new SIDM implementations in OpenGadget3 and AREPO that also allow for multiple scattering events per time step. . Appendix A gives a more detailed description of our scatter treatment including a number of tests that justify this multi-scatter approach. The results obtained with the SphDSMC code are in red, while the green, ocre, azure-blue, and cyan lines show the results obtained with the N N -body code for four different values of the (Plummer) gravitational softening length, ε \varepsilon , as indicated. Here and throughout, all softening lengths are expressed in units of the characteristic radius r s r_{\rm s} . Figure 4: Evolution of the NFWc30 halo for three different values of the collision cross section; σ m = 1 ​ cm 2 ​ g − 1 \sigma_{\rm m}=1\>{\rm cm}^{2}\,{\rm g}^{-1} (left), 10 ​ cm 2 ​ g − 1 10\>{\rm cm}^{2}\,{\rm g}^{-1} (middle) and 200 ​ cm 2 ​ g − 1 200\>{\rm cm}^{2}\,{\rm g}^{-1} (right), corresponding to σ ~ m = 0.16 \tilde{\sigma}_{\rm m}=0.16 , 1.6 1.6 , and 32 32 , respectively. Each halo is evolved with the SphDSMC code using N p = 10 6 N_{\rm p}=10^{6} particles until the core density reaches ρ c = 10 5 ​ ρ s \rho_{\rm c}=10^{5}\rho_{\rm s} . The upper panels show the evolution of the core density, nicely depicting the differences as one transitions from core collapse in the LMFP regime (left) to that in the SMFP regime (right). The three middle rows of panels show the radial profiles of density, 1D velocity dispersion, and the velocity anisotropy parameter. The green and black lines show the initial and final profiles, respectively, while the other coloured lines show the profiles at intermediate times, indicated by vertical lines in the top panels. Finally, the lower panels plot the density at radius r r as a function of the enclosed mass within r r . See text for detailed discussion. In the case of CDM, the various lines are offset from each other along the vertical direction for clarity. As is evident, the results for the SphDSMC code show that the central density remains constant for the duration of the simulation. This is the expected result, given that CDM is collisionless and that the initial conditions were setup in equilibrium. In the case of the N N -body simulations, the central density only remains constant in time for ε = 0.0464 \varepsilon=0.0464 . For smaller softening lengths, the central density decreases over time, by up to ∼ 60 \sim 60 percent in 5 ​ Gyr 5\>{\rm Gyr} in the case with ε = 0.0077 \varepsilon=0.0077 . This is due to insufficient suppression of large-angle scattering between particles, which results in artificial creation of an isothermal core ( Athanassoula et al., 2000 ; Dehnen, 2001 ; Power et al., 2003 ; van den Bosch and Ogiya, 2018 , e.g.,) . In the case of SIDM (top-right panel), the SphDSMC simulation reveals the characteristic gravothermal evolution of a SIDM halo; initially, the central density rapidly declines as the self-interactions convert the central cusp into an extended isothermal constant-density core due to inward conductive heat transfer. Subsequently, the heat starts to flow outward, from the hot central core to the cooler outskirts, triggering a slow but ever-accelerating increase of the central density characteristic of gravothermal core collapse ( Lynden-Bell and Wood, 1968 ; Balberg and Shapiro, 2002 ) . The results for the four N N -body simulations with different softening lengths clearly diverge at late times, with larger softening length causing core collapse to occur later. This dependence on the choice of softening length has previously been reported by Mace et al. (2024) and Palubski et al. (2024) . Interestingly, the N N -body results converge to the results obtained using the SphDSMC code, which does not require any softening, in the limit ε → 0.0077 \varepsilon\to 0.0077 , which is the value for which the CDM simulations reveal strong artificial core formation. We have repeated these tests for (truncated) NFW haloes with different concentrations, and also for the Core halo, always using N p = 10 6 N_{\rm p}=10^{6} particles, and consistently find that the N N -body simulations converge to the results of the SphDSMC simulation when ε → 0.0077 \varepsilon\to 0.0077 , while larger values for ε \varepsilon result in delayed core collapse. This suggests that SIDM simulations require smaller softening lengths than CDM simulations of the same system to properly resolve core collapse. This notion that SIDM simulations may require a smaller softening length than CDM simulations was also hinted at in Fischer et al. (2025) . It is also consistent with Mace et al. (2024) and Palubski et al. (2024) , who recommend using a softening length advocated by van den Bosch and Ogiya (2018) for resolving the tidal evolution of (CDM) subhalos, which is significantly smaller than the softening length that is considered optimal for evolving CDM haloes in isolation ( Power et al., 2003 , for example, as advocated in) . It is worth pointing out that the N N -body simulations are terminated when the central density reaches 10 3 ​ ρ s 10^{3}\rho_{\rm s} . This is done because the simulations, all of which are run on a single core without hierarchical time stepping, become unacceptably slow once the core density exceeds this value. However, with the SphDSMC simulations, which are significantly faster, we can afford to run the simulations to much higher density. For comparison, while the N N -body simulation with ε = 0.0077 \varepsilon=0.0077 took 175 175 hours of wall clock time to complete, the SphDSMC simulation only required 4.7 4.7 hours despite continuing to a central density that is a factor 100 higher. Finally, we emphasize that we are not advocating ε = 0.0077 \varepsilon=0.0077 as the optimal softening when simulating SIDM in general; we have only demonstrated that this yields the best agreement with the SphDSMC results when simulating down to a central density of ∼ 1000 ​ ρ s \sim 1000\rho_{\rm s} . It is to be expected that if we were able to run the N N -body simulations to even higher densities even smaller softening lengths would be required to resolve the central core. Hence, when using a simulation code that requires force softening to study gravothermal collapse deep into the collapse phase, adaptive softening schemes are likely to be required. This highlights an important advantage of the SphDSMC code, which is free of the burden to soften gravity. The panels in the middle row of Fig. 2 show the evolution of | Δ ​ E / E 0 | = | [ E ⁡ ( t ) − E ⁡ ( 0 ) ] / E ⁡ ( 0 ) | |\Delta E/E_{0}|=|[E(t)-E(0)]/E(0)| where E ⁡ ( t ) E(t) is the total energy of the system at time t t . Note that energy conservation in the N N -body simulations is typically at the level of 10 − 4 10^{-4} , with little to no dependence on ε \varepsilon , and is only slightly worse in the case of SIDM than in the case of CDM. As has been pointed out in several recent studies ( Palubski et al., 2024 ; Mace et al., 2024 ; Fischer et al., 2024 ) , achieving such a level of energy conservation with SIDM simulations is extremely challenging when using hierarchical time stepping and/or multiple processors and typically requires extremely small time steps. We are able to avoid these issues by having all particles use the same (adaptive) time step and running the simulations on a single core (see Robertson, 2017 , for a detailed discussion) . Note that energy conservation in the SphDSMC simulations is more than an order of magnitude better than in the N N -body simulations. Given that the SphDSMC simulations run in a fraction of the time, do not require any force softening, and are able to follow the evolution to significantly higher central densities, it is clear that the SphDSMC code is vastly superior to the standard N N -body approach for studying the gravothermal evolution of SIDM haloes, as long as one is willing to accept the restriction of spherical symmetry ( Gurian and May, 2025 ; Kamionkowski et al., 2026 , see also) Finally, the lower-right panel of Fig. 2 shows the ratio of the scatter rate in the simulation to the expected rate. The latter is computed using Γ pred = 1 2 ​ ∫ n ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) ​ ρ ​ ( 𝐱 ) ​ σ m ​ ⟨ v rel ⟩ ​ ( 𝐱 ) ​ d 3 ​ 𝐱 = 8 ​ π ​ N p ​ σ m ​ 1 M tot ​ ∫ 0 ∞ ρ 2 ​ ( r ) ​ v ​ ( r ) ​ r 2 ​ d r , \begin{split}\Gamma_{\rm pred}&=\frac{1}{2}\int n({\bf x})\,\rho({\bf x})\,\sigma_{\rm m}\,\langle v_{\rm rel}\rangle({\bf x})\,{\rm d}^{3}{\bf x}\\ &=8\sqrt{\pi}\,N_{\rm p}\,\sigma_{\rm m}\,\frac{1}{M_{\rm tot}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\rho^{2}(r)\,v(r)\,r^{2}\,{\rm d}r\,,\end{split} (24) where n ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) = ρ ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) / m p n({\bf x})=\rho({\bf x})/m_{\rm p} is the number density of particles, v ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) v({\bf x}) is the local 1D velocity dispersion, and in the second step we have assumed spherical symmetry and that the particles follow a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution. We evaluate Γ pred \Gamma_{\rm pred} every few time steps using the instantaneous density and velocity dispersion profiles of the halo computed on the fly in the simulation codes, and compare its value against the actual scatter rate in the simulation. The latter is evaluated as Γ sim = ( ∑ i N scat , i ) / Δ ​ t \Gamma_{\rm sim}=(\sum_{i}N_{{\rm scat},i})/\Delta t , where N scat , i N_{{\rm scat},i} is the number of scatter events that particle i i experienced during the time period Δ ​ t \Delta t . Note that the scatter rates in both the N N -body and SphDSMC codes are in excellent agreement with the theoretical predictions to within the shot noise 6 6 6 This noise becomes large during the later stages of the core collapse as a consequence of the fact that the time steps become progressively smaller. , justifying the Monte-Carlo scatter algorithms in both codes. As an additional validation of the SphDSMC code, we simulate the gravothermal evolution of the Core ∗ halo with σ m = 25 ​ cm 2 ​ g − 1 \sigma_{\rm m}=25\>{\rm cm}^{2}\,{\rm g}^{-1} using both the N N -body code and the SphDSMC code. Fig. 3 shows snapshots of the density profiles (top panels), and the radial profiles of the 1D velocity dispersion v = ( σ r 2 + σ t 2 ) / 3 v=\sqrt{(\sigma^{2}_{\rm r}+\sigma^{2}_{\rm t})/3} (25) with σ x 2 = ⟨ v x 2 ⟩ − ⟨ v x ⟩ 2 \sigma^{2}_{x}=\langle v_{x}^{2}\rangle-\langle v_{x}\rangle^{2} (middle panels) and the velocity anisotropy parameter β ani ≡ 1 − σ t 2 2 ​ σ r 2 , \beta_{\rm ani}\equiv 1-{\sigma^{2}_{\rm t}\over 2\sigma^{2}_{\rm r}}\,, (26) (bottom panels). Results are shown at four different times, as indicated. Note the excellent agreement between the N N -body results (blue curves) and those obtained using the completely independent SphDSMC code (orange curves). Also note the development of a large ‘bump’ in the velocity dispersion profile at large radii. This feature is due to particles that receive large velocity kicks due to scattering in the dense central region that propels them to highly radial orbits ( Giersz and Heggie, 1994 ; Takahashi, 1995 ; Koda and Shapiro, 2011 ; Fischer et al., 2025 ; Gurian and May, 2025 , see also) . This is supported by the β ani \beta_{\rm ani} profiles, which show that the halo outskirts become highly radially anisotropic. The core itself, on the other hand, remains, at all times, perfectly isotropic ( β ani = 0 \beta_{\rm ani}=0 ), as expected for elastic short-range interactions. For comparison, the violet dashed curves show the predictions obtained using the GTF code with the best-fit conductivity model presented in Section 3.4 . Although the GTF results accurately match the density profiles at all times, they do not reproduce the bump-feature in the velocity distribution. This is a consequence of the fact that the GTF code is inherently 1D and therefore implicitly assumes velocity isotropy throughout.

sections.heading: 3.2 Gravothermal evolution in the long and short mean free path regimes
sections.text: We now use the SphDSMC code to study the gravothermal evolution of SIDM haloes in both the long and the short mean free path regimes. Fig. 4 shows the evolution of a NFWc30 halo for three different values of the collision cross section; σ m = 1 ​ cm 2 ​ g − 1 \sigma_{\rm m}=1\>{\rm cm}^{2}\,{\rm g}^{-1} , 10 ​ cm 2 ​ g − 1 10\>{\rm cm}^{2}\,{\rm g}^{-1} and 200 ​ cm 2 ​ g − 1 200\>{\rm cm}^{2}\,{\rm g}^{-1} , as indicated. This corresponds to dimensionless cross sections of σ ~ m = 0.16 \tilde{\sigma}_{\rm m}=0.16 , 1.6 1.6 , and 32 32 , respectively. Each halo is evolved with the SphDSMC code using N p = 10 6 N_{\rm p}=10^{6} particles until the core density reaches ρ c = 10 5 ​ ρ s \rho_{\rm c}=10^{5}\rho_{\rm s} . The upper panels show the evolution of the core density. For σ m = 1 ​ cm 2 ​ g − 1 \sigma_{\rm m}=1\>{\rm cm}^{2}\,{\rm g}^{-1} (left panels), the evolution is characteristic of gravothermal evolution in the LMFP regime; rapid core formation, followed by a slow, but ever accelerating core collapse. During the final stages, the increase in the core density is catastrophic (i.e., faster than exponential). For σ m = 10 ​ cm 2 ​ g − 1 \sigma_{\rm m}=10\>{\rm cm}^{2}\,{\rm g}^{-1} (middle panels), the core collapse is more gradual; although the time to reach ρ c = 10 5 ​ ρ s \rho_{\rm c}=10^{5}\rho_{\rm s} is roughly six times shorter than in the case with σ m = 1 ​ cm 2 ​ g − 1 \sigma_{\rm m}=1\>{\rm cm}^{2}\,{\rm g}^{-1} , the rate at which the core density is increasing at that stage is significantly slower. This trend continues to larger cross sections; for σ m = 200 ​ cm 2 ​ g − 1 \sigma_{\rm m}=200\>{\rm cm}^{2}\,{\rm g}^{-1} (right panels), the entire region inside 3.5 ​ r s 3.5r_{\rm s} is already in the SMFP regime (i.e., Kn < 1 {\rm Kn}<1 ) from the start of the simulation. Following core formation, ρ c \rho_{\rm c} grows (only) at a close-to-exponential rate, and it actually takes almost twice as long to reach a core density of 10 5 ​ ρ s 10^{5}\rho_{\rm s} as in the case with the 20-fold smaller cross section. Figure 5: The upper panel plots the ratio t 3 / t 0 t_{3}/t_{0} as a function of the dimensionless cross section, σ ~ m \tilde{\sigma}_{\rm m} . Coloured circles correspond to the results from the SphDSMC simulations for different values of the halo concentration parameter, as indicated. Blue and cyan lines are predictions obtained with the GTF code for different combinations of the parameters α \alpha and β \beta , as indicated. The black dotted line shows the results for the fitting function given by equations ( 28 ) with the best-fit parameters of Table 2. The lower panels shows the residuals with respect to this fitting function, with the grey-shaded band indicating the [ − 2 ​ σ , + 2 ​ σ ] [-2\sigma,+2\sigma] band, where σ \sigma is the standard deviation in collapse times due to realisation noise (see Appendix B ). The notion that core-collapse behaves differently in the long- and short mean free path regimes has previously been emphasized and demonstrated using gravothermal fluid codes ( Balberg and Shapiro, 2002 ; Balberg et al., 2002 ; Gad-Nasr et al., 2024 ) . However, to our knowledge, it has never been demonstrated or confirmed in numerical simulations, with the exception of Koda and Shapiro (2011) and Mace et al. (2026) who ran simulations with σ ~ m \tilde{\sigma}_{\rm m} values as large as unity and noted that such systems already deviate from the self-similar evolution characteristic of the LMFP regime (see discussion at the end of Section 3.3 ). The main reason why most studies based on N N -body simulations have focussed on small values of σ ~ m \tilde{\sigma}_{\rm m} is that it is extremely expensive to evolve a system in the SMFP regime. While this remains true for the SphDSMC code, it is still feasible to evolve systems with moderate σ ~ m \tilde{\sigma}_{\rm m} (up to ∼ 30 \sim 30 ) up to relatively high densities. The reason for the different behaviour in the long and short mean free path regimes is well understood ( Balberg et al., 2002 ) . Once the core becomes optically thick, i.e., when the mean free path λ mfp = 1 / ( ρ ​ σ m ) \lambda_{\rm mfp}=1/(\rho\sigma_{\rm m}) becomes smaller than the size of the core, it can only transfer heat to the envelope at its surface boundary. Prior to this, the entire core can directly transfer heat, resulting in much more efficient heat transport. This is also evident from the expressions for the conductivities; κ LMFP ∝ σ m \kappa_{\rm LMFP}\propto\sigma_{\rm m} (equation [ 19 ]) while κ SMFP ∝ 1 / σ m \kappa_{\rm SMFP}\propto 1/\sigma_{\rm m} (equation [ 18 ]). The three middle rows of panels of Fig. 4 show the radial profiles of density, 1D velocity dispersion, and the velocity anisotropy parameter, respectively. The green and black lines show the initial and final profiles. The other coloured lines show the profiles at intermediate times, indicated by vertical lines in the top panels. Note how the initial cusp is first converted to an isothermal core, after which the core contracts, increasing its density and central velocity dispersion. Although, by construction, the final density profiles all have ρ c = 10 5 ​ ρ s \rho_{\rm c}=10^{5}\rho_{\rm s} , the detailed profiles show a clear dependence on σ m \sigma_{\rm m} . In particular, when σ m \sigma_{\rm m} is large, the density at intermediate radii (roughly around r / r s = 1 r/r_{\rm s}=1 ) ends up being significantly lower than its initial value. The velocity dispersion profiles also show clear differences, with the core ending up hotter for larger cross sections, even though the core densities at the end are identical. Similarly to the case of the Core ∗ halo shown in Fig. 3 , over time a ‘bump’ appears in the velocity dispersion profile at larger radii, albeit much weaker this time; it is most clearly evident in the case of σ m = 200 ​ cm 2 ​ g − 1 \sigma_{\rm m}=200\>{\rm cm}^{2}\,{\rm g}^{-1} . Finally, the lower panels of Fig. 4 plot the density at radius r r as a function of the enclosed mass within r r . This nicely illustrates the different core structures in the LMFP and SMFP regimes. In particular, in the latter, one can infer a clear core-within-a-core structure ( Balberg et al., 2002 ; Feng et al., 2021 , see also) . This inner core, which becomes denser over time, is entirely in the SMFP regime and only transfers heat to the outer core structure from its surface. The vast majority of heat flux is highly localised at this boundary of the inner core. As shown in Balberg et al. (2002) , in this regime the core mass therefore decreases much slower than in the LMFP regime ( Gad-Nasr et al., 2024 , see also) .

sections.heading: 3.3 The Gravothermal evolution of NFW haloes
sections.text: We now compare the results obtained with our SphDSMC code with those obtained using the GTF code. As mentioned in Section 1 this requires a calibration of the conductivity in the LMFP regime, which is characterised by the free parameter β \beta (cf. equation [ 19 ]). It is common to calibrate β \beta by comparing the time-scales for collapse. Unfortunately, when σ m \sigma_{\rm m} is large and core collapse occurs largely in the SMFP regime, there is no well-defined time of core collapse, given that d ​ log ⁡ ρ c / d ​ log ⁡ t {\rm d}\log\rho_{\rm c}/{\rm d}\log t is much smaller (cf. upper-right panel of Fig. 4 ). Therefore, we instead calibrate the GTF model using the time t 3 t_{3} , defined as the time when the core density 7 7 7 We have also performed this analysis using the alternative definition of core density, ρ − 2 \rho_{-2} (see Section 2.5 ), which yields similar results. ρ c \rho_{\rm c} reaches a value of 10 3 ​ ρ s 10^{3}\rho_{\rm s} . In what follows, we will loosely refer to t 3 t_{3} as the collapse time. We use the SphDSMC code to evolve a set of spherical isotropic NFW haloes with different concentrations (haloes NFWc10, NFWc30 and NFWc50 listed in Table 1) and different collision cross sections. Each halo has 10 6 10^{6} particles and is truncated such that M tot = 2 ​ M vir M_{\rm tot}=2M_{\rm vir} . The coloured dots in the upper panel of Fig. 5 show the ratio t 3 / t 0 t_{3}/t_{0} , where t 0 t_{0} is the collisional relaxation time given by equation ( 3 ), as a function of the dimensionless collision cross section σ ~ m ≡ σ m / σ s \tilde{\sigma}_{\rm m}\equiv\sigma_{\rm m}/\sigma_{\rm s} . Different colours correspond to different halo concentrations, as indicated. Note that t 3 / t 0 t_{3}/t_{0} is roughly constant for σ ~ m ∼ < 0.1 \tilde{\sigma}_{\rm m}\lower 3.01385pt\hbox{$\;\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\sim}\limits^{<}}\;$}0.1 , but increases rapidly for larger cross sections. Importantly, the trend is independent of halo concentration. Next, we run the GTF code for the NFWc30 halo (results for other halo concentrations are identical) on a fine grid of σ ~ m \tilde{\sigma}_{\rm m} . We initially adopt the standard interpolation scheme for conductivity, given by equation ( 20 ), and tune β \beta to fit the results for small σ ~ m \tilde{\sigma}_{\rm m} (i.e., in the LMFP regime). This results in a best-fit value of β = 0.90 \beta=0.90 , which produces the predictions for t 3 / t 0 t_{3}/t_{0} shown as the cyan line in Fig. 5 . As is evident, this drastically underestimates t 3 / t 0 t_{3}/t_{0} for σ ~ m ∼ > 0.1 \tilde{\sigma}_{\rm m}\lower 3.01385pt\hbox{$\;\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\sim}\limits^{>}}\;$}0.1 . Figure 6: The core collapse time t 3 t_{3} as a function of the total mass of the truncated NFWc20 halo, M tot M_{\rm tot} , in units of M vir M_{\rm vir} . Smaller values of M tot / M vir M_{\rm tot}/M_{\rm vir} imply a smaller truncation radius, while an untruncated NFW halo has M tot / M vir → ∞ M_{\rm tot}/M_{\rm vir}\to\infty . Coloured dots indicate results obtained using SphDSMC simulations with N p = 10 6 N_{\rm p}=10^{6} for three different values of the collision cross section, as indicated. Blue lines are predictions obtained using the GTF code with ( α , β ) = ( 0.5 , 0.0.90 ) (\alpha,\beta)=(0.5,0.0.90) , which accurately match the simulation results for any level of truncation. In principle, for each σ m \sigma_{\rm m} one could find a different value for β \beta for which the GTF code reproduces the results of the SphDSMC simulation, and this is largely what has been done in the literature. We find that the range of β \beta values needed to fit the SphDSMC simulation results 8 8 8 For σ ~ m ≲ 2 \tilde{\sigma}_{\rm m}\lesssim 2 , t 3 ∝ β − 1 t_{3}\propto\beta^{-1} , but for larger cross sections the dependence is weaker, roughly becoming t 3 ∝ β − 0.1 t_{3}\propto\beta^{-0.1} for σ ~ m = 40 \tilde{\sigma}_{\rm m}=40 ranges from 0.90 0.90 for σ ~ m ∼ < 0.1 \tilde{\sigma}_{\rm m}\lower 3.01385pt\hbox{$\;\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\sim}\limits^{<}}\;$}0.1 to ∼ 0.4 \sim 0.4 for σ ~ m = 4 \tilde{\sigma}_{\rm m}=4 . Interestingly, this covers pretty much the entire range of values for β \beta that have been obtained by fitting results obtained with GTF codes to N N -body simulations of NFW haloes, which include values for β \beta ranging from 0.9 0.9 ( Zhong et al., 2023 ; Mace et al., 2026 ) to 0.6 0.6 ( Essig et al., 2019 ; Outmezguine et al., 2023 ) . The lack of even smaller values of β \beta is likely the result of the fact that they correspond to relatively large values of σ ~ m \tilde{\sigma}_{\rm m} , which have not been considered for N N -body simulations given that the CPU requirements are too demanding. Comparing equations ( 18 ) and ( 19 ), it is clear that β \beta is some measure of the effective impact parameter. Hence, while it is expected that β \beta depends on the detailed density and/or velocity profile of the halo in question (see Section 3.4 ), it makes little sense that it would depend on the collision cross section. Hence, the discrepancy for σ ~ m ∼ > 0.1 \tilde{\sigma}_{\rm m}\lower 3.01385pt\hbox{$\;\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\sim}\limits^{>}}\;$}0.1 is unlikely to be related to β \beta , but rather to the functional form used to interpolate the conductivity parameter between the LMFP and SMFP regimes. As discussed in Section 2.3 , virtually all studies of SIDM haloes based on the gravothermal fluid equations have adopted the interpolation scheme of equation ( 20 ) originally introduced by Balberg et al. (2002) . Here, we generalize this interpolation scheme according to κ = [ κ SMFP − α + κ LMFP − α ] − 1 / α \kappa=\left[\kappa_{\rm SMFP}^{-\alpha}+\kappa_{\rm LMFP}^{-\alpha}\right]^{-1/\alpha} (27) where we treat α \alpha as an additional free parameter. We have experimented with a range of α \alpha values, each time keeping β \beta fixed to 0.90 0.90 . The blue curve in Fig. 5 shows the results for α = 0.5 \alpha=0.5 , which is an excellent match to the data. Hence, using a simple modification of the interpolation scheme, the GTF code accurately reproduces the simulation results for all NFW haloes, regardless of σ m \sigma_{\rm m} or halo concentration. For completeness, we point out that early work by Koda and Shapiro (2011) already noted a discrepancy in the gravothermal evolution of SIDM haloes in the SMFP regime between N N -body simulations and predictions based on the gravothermal fluid equations. However, rather than modifying the interpolation scheme, they suggested modifying the value of the effective impact parameter b b that appears in the expression for the conductivity in the SMFP regime given by equation ( 18 ). In particular, they suggest setting b = 0.25 b=0.25 in the transitional regime where Kn ∼ 1 {\rm Kn}\sim 1 , as opposed to adopting b = 25 ​ π / 32 ≈ 1.385 b=25\sqrt{\pi}/32\approx 1.385 as appropriate for the SMFP regime ( Chapman and Cowling, 1970 ; Lifshitz and Pitaevskii, 1981 ) . More recently, Mace et al. (2026) noticed that reproducing their SIDM core collapse N N -body simulations with predictions from a GTF code requires making the parameter β \beta dependent on the cross section, qualitatively in agreement with the results shown in Fig. 5 . They advocate the use of an ‘effective’ conductivity parameter β eff ​ ( σ ~ m ) \beta_{\rm eff}(\tilde{\sigma}_{m}) , defined such that the conductivity κ = κ LMFP \kappa=\kappa_{\rm LMFP} , with κ LMFP \kappa_{\rm LMFP} given by equation ( 19 ) but with β \beta replaced by β eff \beta_{\rm eff} . Hence, they attempt to characterise the conductivity in the SMFP using the expression for the LMFP regime by making the parameter β \beta dependent on the cross section. They even advocate using a more general interpolation scheme of the form of equation ( 27 ), which they use to derive the functional form of β eff ​ ( σ ~ m ) \beta_{\rm eff}(\tilde{\sigma}_{m}) and then tune α \alpha and β \beta to match their N N -body results. While these modifications suggested by Koda and Shapiro (2011) and Mace et al. (2026) achieve the same goal (tuning GTF results to match simulation results), we consider our solution of modifying the interpolation scheme more elegant. In addition, neither Koda and Shapiro (2011) nor Mace et al. (2026) included simulations with σ ~ m > 1 \tilde{\sigma}_{\rm m}>1 , which limits their ability to probe the SMFP regime. In contrast, our analysis extends all the way to σ ~ m ≈ 20 \tilde{\sigma}_{\rm m}\approx 20 , allowing for a calibration across a much larger dynamic range.

sections.heading: 3.4 Dependence on density profile
sections.text: In the previous section, we have shown that the GTF code accurately describes the gravothermal evolution of an SIDM halo with an initial NFW density profile, for any collision cross section, as long as the conductivity is modelled using ( α , β ) = ( 0.5 , 0.9 ) (\alpha,\beta)=(0.5,0.9) . We now examine whether the same conductivity model also works for haloes with other initial density profiles. We first consider NFW profiles that are truncated differently. Until now, we have exclusively focused on haloes that were truncated such that M tot / M vir = 2 M_{\rm tot}/M_{\rm vir}=2 . The coloured dots in Fig. 6 show the collapse time, t 3 t_{3} , obtained with SphDSMC simulations, for the NFWc20 halo as a function of the ratio M tot / M vir M_{\rm tot}/M_{\rm vir} . Smaller values of M tot / M vir M_{\rm tot}/M_{\rm vir} imply a truncation at smaller radii, whereas M tot / M vir → ∞ M_{\rm tot}/M_{\rm vir}\to\infty for an untruncated NFW profile. Note that all haloes have N p = 10 6 N_{\rm p}=10^{6} particles, independent of their level of truncation. Different colours correspond to different values of the collision cross section, as indicated. Note that more truncated haloes undergo core collapse sooner, in agreement with Nishikawa et al. (2020) , and that the collapse time asymptotes to a constant value for M tot / M vir ∼ > 1.5 M_{\rm tot}/M_{\rm vir}\lower 3.01385pt\hbox{$\;\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\sim}\limits^{>}}\;$}1.5 . Hence, the results for M tot / M vir = 2 M_{\rm tot}/M_{\rm vir}=2 shown in the previous sections are also applicable to untruncated NFW haloes. Figure 7: Same as Fig. 5 , but for the Core halo. Accurately fitting the SphDSMC simulation data (red dots) requires a small adjustment to the parameters α \alpha and β \beta that quantify the conductivity in the GTF model, compared to the parameters that best-fit the results for NFW haloes. The residuals in the lower panel are with respect to the GTF predictions. The blue curves indicate the predicted collapse times obtained by using the GTF code with ( α , β ) = ( 0.5 , 0.9 ) (\alpha,\beta)=(0.5,0.9) . As is evident, this adequately matches the simulation results. Although the fit is not perfect, with the GTF model slightly overpredicting t 3 t_{3} for strongly truncated haloes and small σ ~ m \tilde{\sigma}_{\rm m} , the discrepancy is only at the few percent-level. Hence, we conclude that the fiducial conductivity model with ( α , β ) = ( 0.5 , 0.9 ) (\alpha,\beta)=(0.5,0.9) accurately accounts for the gravothermal collapse of any NFW halo, independent of halo concentration or the level by which the halo has been truncated. sections.heading: 3.5 Unsolved issues regarding gravothermal evolution deep into the SMFP regime
sections.text: As is evident from the bottom panel of Fig. 5 , the GTF model predicts collapse times that are somewhat larger than in the simulations, by up to 10 10 percent. This discrepancy is also apparent in Fig. 8 , which shows the evolution of core density ρ c \rho_{\rm c} (left panels) and core velocity dispersion v c v_{\rm c} (right panels), for the NFWc30 halo for four different values of σ m \sigma_{\rm m} , as indicated. The azure-blue lines show the results obtained with the SphDSMC code, while the black dashed lines indicate the results of the GTF code with ( α , β ) = ( 0.5 , 0.9 ) (\alpha,\beta)=(0.5,0.9) . For clarity, the time axis is normalised by the value of t 3 t_{3} inferred from the SphDSMC simulation. Overall, the agreement is very good. However, for large σ m \sigma_{\rm m} and at late times the GTF code seems to predict somewhat lower densities and velocity dispersions than the SphDSMC simulations. We have verified that these discrepancies are not manifestations of realisation noise (cf. Appendix B ), and that they are robust to changes in the time stepping criteria used in the simulations (i.e., changes in η \eta or ζ \zeta ) or to changes in the spatial or temporal resolution of the GTF code. We suspect instead that the discrepancy is due to the limited mass resolution of the SphDSMC simulations. As discussed in Section 2.2.1 , as the central density of a halo undergoing core collapse increases, there comes a point in time when the SphDSMC code can no longer resolve the mean-free path in the central region. As long as the spatial extent r fail r_{\rm fail} , over which this is the case is small compared to the core radius, this should not have a major impact, given that the core is largely homogeneous and isotropic. However, if r fail r_{\rm fail} becomes larger than or comparable to the core radius, the core will transport too much of its heat outward, thereby accelerating its collapse. The yellow shaded regions indicate the times when r fail > r c r_{\rm fail}>r_{\rm c} . This roughly coincides with the times when the densities and velocity dispersions of the SphDSMC simulations exceed the GTF predictions, supporting our hypothesis However, there is also an alternative explanation for the discrepancy, first pointed out by Gurian and May (2025) . Due to the development of velocity anisotropy in the simulations, something that is not captured by the GTF code, heat transfer is no longer restricted to conduction, but can also arise from viscous dissipation of anisotropic stress (simply put, the stress tensor is no longer diagonal). In this case, there is excess heat transfer, not due to a lack of spatial resolution, but due to a real physical process that is accounted for in the SphDSMC simulations but not in the GTF code. Fig. 9 compares the radial profiles of the evolving NFWc30 halo obtained using the SphDSMC code (solid lines) and the newly calibrated GTF code (dashed lines). Similarly to Fig. 4 , the results are shown for three different collision cross sections, as indicated, and the top panels show the temporal evolution of the core density. As in Fig. 8 , the yellow shaded regions indicate the times when r fail > r c r_{\rm fail}>r_{\rm c} . The bottom panels show the profiles of density, 1D velocity dispersion, and the anisotropy parameter as a function of the enclosed mass. Each panel shows three profiles; the initial profile at t = 0 t=0 (blue and cyan-dashed), an intermediate profile corresponding to ρ c ∼ 300 ​ ρ s \rho_{\rm c}\sim 300\rho_{\rm s} (violet and pink-dashed), and a final profile corresponding to ρ c = 10,000 ​ ρ s \rho_{\rm c}=10,000\rho_{\rm s} (black and green-dashed). In most cases, the profiles obtained using the GTF code (dashed curves) are in good agreement with those from the SphDSMC simulation. However, the final profiles for σ m = 200 ​ cm 2 ​ g − 1 \sigma_{\rm m}=200\>{\rm cm}^{2}\,{\rm g}^{-1} reveal large discrepancies; the core-within-a-core structure is clearly more pronounced in the GTF density profile than in that inferred from the SphDSMC simulation. The inner GTF core is also hotter and smaller. Similar, albeit smaller, discrepancies are also apparent in the final profiles for σ m = 1.0 ​ cm 2 ​ g − 1 \sigma_{\rm m}=1.0\>{\rm cm}^{2}\,{\rm g}^{-1} and σ m = 10 ​ cm 2 ​ g − 1 \sigma_{\rm m}=10\>{\rm cm}^{2}\,{\rm g}^{-1} ( Gurian and May, 2025 , see also) . If these discrepancies are due to viscous heat transfer that is not accounted for in the GTF code, we expect to see a significant velocity anisotropy where the discrepancies are apparent. Upon close inspection of Fig. 9 , it is evident that the velocity distributions in the SphDSMC simulations seem to become radially anisotropic at just about the region where the discrepancy arises. Although this supports the hypothesis that the discrepancies arise as a consequence of viscous dissipation of anisotropic stress, the alternative explanation, that they arise as a consequence of inadequate spatial resolution in the SphDSMC simulations, cannot be ruled out. After all, as is apparent from the top panels, the discrepancies seem to be present only when r fail > r c r_{\rm fail}>r_{\rm c} . Gurian and May (2025) tested the viscosity-hypothesis by explicitly demonstrating that the heat flow in their KiSS-SIDM simulation (similar to the SphDSMC simulations used here) is inconsistent with that expected according to the gravothermal fluid equations. They then argue that ”this deviation is naturally explained by viscous dissipation sourced in the intermediate mean-free-path regime”. While true, it can also be explained by heat transfer that is artificially too large in the KiSS-SIDM simulation due to insufficient spatial resolution. Hence, we conclude that it is currently unclear whether the discrepancies shown here and in Gurian and May (2025) arise from artificially enhanced heat transport due to a lack of spatial resolution in the SphDSMC simulations or from viscous heat transport that is not accounted for in the GTF code. In principle, one could discriminate between these two alternatives by comparing simulations of different mass resolutions. If the lack of spatial resolution is the main cause of the discrepancy, simulations with smaller (larger) N p N_{\rm p} , should start to deviate from the GTF predictions at earlier (later) times. If, instead, the discrepancy is due to viscous dissipation, it should be largely independent of N p N_{\rm p} . Unfortunately, this test is hampered by the fact that for N p < 10 6 N_{\rm p}<10^{6} realisation noise becomes too large (see Appendix B ), while simulations with N p > 10 6 N_{\rm p}>10^{6} quickly become too CPU intensive.

sections.heading: 4.1 Forming seed black holes with SIDM core collapse
sections.text: If nothing can stop the gravothermal catastrophe, the consensus is that the core will ultimately become relativistic, triggering an instability that causes the direct collapse to a BH. In what follows, we define t BH t_{\rm BH} as the time it takes for a halo’s core velocity dispersion, v c v_{\rm c} , to become equal to c / 3 c/3 , with c c the speed of light, which we assume to coincide with the time of BH formation. In the LMFP regime, the core density rises at a super-exponential rate. It is therefore tempting, but incorrect (see below), to assume that the core density will continue to increase at this same rate until the core becomes relativistic and collapses to a black hole. In this context, Pollack et al. (2015) reported a time-scale for catastrophic collapse to a black hole of t BH = 455.65 ​ t 0 t_{\rm BH}=455.65\,t_{0} for a fiducial isolated NFW halo. Based on the self-similarity of gravothermal collapse in the LMFP regime, Essig et al. (2019) derived a core-collapse time of t cc = 150 β ​ 1 σ m ​ ρ s ​ r s ​ 1 4 ​ π ​ G ​ ρ s . t_{\rm cc}={150\over\beta}\,{1\over\sigma_{\rm m}\,\rho_{\rm s}\,r_{\rm s}}\,{1\over\sqrt{4\pi G\rho_{\rm s}}}\,. (32) which can be rewritten as t cc = 150 β ​ 1 σ ~ m ​ t core = 338.5 β ​ t 0 . t_{\rm cc}={150\over\beta}\,{1\over\tilde{\sigma}_{\rm m}}\,t_{\rm core}={338.5\over\beta}\,t_{0}\,. (33) Using β = 0.75 \beta=0.75 , which is a typical value that is often quoted, this translates to t cc = 451.35 ​ t 0 t_{\rm cc}=451.35t_{0} , very similar to the value obtained by Pollack et al. (2015) . Using β = 0.9 \beta=0.9 , which is the value advocated here, this yields t cc = 376.1 ​ t 0 t_{\rm cc}=376.1t_{0} which is a good match to equation ( 28 ), but only for sufficiently small σ ~ m \tilde{\sigma}_{\rm m} . In recent years, numerous studies have used equation ( 32 ) to model the time-scale for core collapse and have assumed that this coincides with the time-scale on which core collapse produces a seed BH ( Choquette et al., 2019 ; Shah and Adhikari, 2024 ; Roberts et al., 2025a ; Roberts et al., 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ) . However, as clearly stressed by Balberg et al. (2002) , Essig et al. (2019) and others, and as evident from Fig. 10 , this self-similar scaling is only valid in the LMFP regime, an important constraint that seems to have been overlooked on more than one occasion. A proper derivation of t BH t_{\rm BH} needs to account for the fact that any collapsing core becomes optically thick (and thus enters the SMFP regime) before it becomes relativistic. And when the core is no longer in the LMFP regime, its density and velocity dispersion increase much slower. As a consequence, the core collapse time given by equation ( 32 ), which is only valid in the LMFP regime, can severely underestimate t BH t_{\rm BH} . To illustrate this point, the solid green line in the right-hand panel of Fig. 10 indicates t cc t_{\rm cc} obtained using equation ( 32 ) with β = 0.90 \beta=0.90 . This accurately fits the results of our GTF calculations, but only for σ ~ m ∼ < 0.1 \tilde{\sigma}_{\rm m}\lower 3.01385pt\hbox{$\;\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\sim}\limits^{<}}\;$}0.1 . For larger cross sections, equation ( 32 ) drastically underestimates t n t_{n} , for any n n . Relating this to the time-scale for BH formation requires computing the core density at the time the velocity dispersion of the core becomes relativistic (i.e., when v c ≃ c / 3 v_{\rm c}\simeq c/3 ), which we address in detail in a follow-up paper (Tokayer & van den Bosch, in prep.). Here we present a rough estimate based on Gad-Nasr et al. (2024) , who, using a GTF code, find that during the late stages of gravothermal collapse, when the core is well in the SMFP regime, the density and velocity dispersion of the core evolve according to d ​ log ⁡ ρ c / d ​ log ⁡ v c ∼ 10 {\rm d}\log\rho_{\rm c}/{\rm d}\log v_{\rm c}\sim 10 . Let ρ n = 10 n ​ ρ s \rho_{n}=10^{n}\rho_{\rm s} and v n v_{n} be the density and velocity dispersion of the core when it reaches this stage. Then, the core density at the moment the core becomes relativistic is given by log ⁡ ( ρ c ρ s ) = n + d ​ log ⁡ ρ c d ​ log ⁡ v c ​ log ⁡ ( c / 3 v n ) \log\left({\rho_{\rm c}\over\rho_{\rm s}}\right)=n+{{\rm d}\log\rho_{\rm c}\over{\rm d}\log v_{\rm c}}\log\left({c/3\over v_{n}}\right) (34) As an example, consider the NFWc30 halo with a collision cross section of σ m = 200 ​ cm 2 ​ g − 1 \sigma_{\rm m}=200\>{\rm cm}^{2}\,{\rm g}^{-1} . As is evident from the right-hand panels of Fig. 8 , when this system reaches a core density ρ c = 10 5 ​ ρ s \rho_{\rm c}=10^{5}\rho_{\rm s} , the velocity dispersion of the core has reached v c ≈ v s = 566.41 ​ km ​ s − 1 v_{\rm c}\approx v_{\rm s}=566.41\>{\rm km}\,{\rm s}^{-1} . Since σ ~ m = 32 \tilde{\sigma}_{\rm m}=32 , it is well into the SMFP regime at this point in time, and we may therefore assume that the core will continue to evolve obeying d ​ log ⁡ ρ c / d ​ log ⁡ v c ∼ 10 {\rm d}\log\rho_{\rm c}/{\rm d}\log v_{\rm c}\sim 10 . Using equation ( 34 ), we infer that log ⁡ ( ρ c / ρ s ) ≈ 27.5 \log(\rho_{\rm c}/\rho_{\rm s})\approx 27.5 . Thus, we can estimate the time for BH formation as t BH = t n t_{\rm BH}=t_{n} with n = 27.5 n=27.5 . Using the fitting function given by equations ( 28 )-( 29 ), this yields t BH = 3.26 × 10 6 ​ t 0 t_{\rm BH}=3.26\times 10^{6}t_{0} , orders of magnitude larger than simply equating t BH t_{\rm BH} with t cc t_{\rm cc} as in numerous previous studies. In particular, although the collisional relaxation time for the NFWc30 halo listed in Table 1 is only t 0 = 0.186 ​ Myr t_{0}=0.186\>{\rm Myr} (at z = 0 z=0 ), it will take a staggering 604.9 ​ Gyr 604.9\>{\rm Gyr} for this halo to collapse to form a seed BH. Recently, Gu et al. (2026) presented a new method for solving the gravothermal fluid equations that allows them to follow the core collapse of SIDM haloes to the point of BH formation by incorporating general relativistic effects through the Misner-Sharp formalism. They model the conductivity using the standard interpolation scheme ( α = 1.0 \alpha=1.0 ) with β = 0.75 \beta=0.75 , and apply their formalism to an NFW halo with ρ s = 0.019 ​ M ⊙ ​ pc − 3 \rho_{\rm s}=0.019\>{\rm M_{\odot}}\>{\rm pc}^{-3} , r s = 2.6 ​ kpc r_{\rm s}=2.6\>{\rm kpc} and v s = 83.6 ​ km ​ s − 1 v_{\rm s}=83.6\>{\rm km}\,{\rm s}^{-1} , and using a collision cross section σ m = 5 ​ cm 2 ​ g − 1 \sigma_{\rm m}=5\>{\rm cm}^{2}\,{\rm g}^{-1} which implies σ ~ m = 0.052 \tilde{\sigma}_{\rm m}=0.052 . As expected, the system starts in the LMFP regime with a phase of super-exponential core collapse at t ≈ 450 ​ t 0 t\approx 450t_{0} . However, once the core becomes optically thick, the rate at which the core density increases slows down significantly. Using a multi-stage approach, in which the authors repeatedly zoom in to smaller and smaller scales, they are able to follow the collapse all the way up to horizon crossing, which occurs at t BH = 580 ​ t 0 t_{\rm BH}=580t_{0} . This confirms that equation ( 32 ) underestimates the time-scale for BH formation, since it does not account for the fact that at some point the core always becomes optically thick. Since σ ~ m \tilde{\sigma}_{\rm m} is very small, this happens at a relatively late stage, when ρ c \rho_{\rm c} is already very large.
