sections.heading: 5 Conclusions
sections.text: We have studied the gravothermal evolution of SIDM haloes using a new spherical Direct Simulation Monte Carlo code called SphDSMC that is similar to the kinetic solver KiSS-SIDM recently developed by Gurian and May (2025) and to the NSphere code developed independently by Kamionkowski and Sigurdson (2026) . SphDSMC assumes spherical symmetry and integrates the radial coordinates of particles in an N N -body system, while treating collisional scattering using the Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method of Bird (1994) . The main advantages of this method are (i) that it is much faster than the N N -body method, (ii) that it does not require any particle softening, (iii) that it allows integration to much higher central densities, and (iv) that it typically results in much better energy conservation than standard N N -body codes. The main shortcoming of SphDSMC is that it only works for spherically symmetric systems. We have compared the results obtained with SphDSMC with those obtained using the standard N N -body method. The results of the latter converge to those obtained with SphDSMC for small softening lengths, significantly smaller (roughly by a factor of four) than what is considered ideal for CDM simulations, in the sense that running the same system without self-interactions causes artificial core formation due to inadequate suppression of two-body interactions. We have also demonstrated (Appendix A ) that multiple scattering events can be allowed per time step in N N -body simulations, despite many claims in the literature to the contrary. A comparison of SphDSMC with results obtained using a GTF code that solves the gravothermal fluid equations shows that the standard harmonic scheme used to interpolate the conductivity between the long- and short-mean-free paths is inaccurate. Allowing for a more gentle transition between these two regimes yields results that are in perfect agreement with the SphDSMC results. In particular, we show that a single value for the parameter that controls the conductivity in the LMFP regime can reproduce the results for any NFW halo, independent of halo concentration or the extent to which the halo has been truncated. The fact that all studies to date have adopted an inaccurate interpolation function explains why there is a large discrepancy in the literature as to the value of this free parameter. The best-fit parameters that quantify the conductivity κ ⁡ ( σ m ) \kappa(\sigma_{\rm m}) show a weak dependence on the detailed density profile of the halo in question. Hence, it is recommended that these parameters be calibrated against simulation results for density profiles other than those considered here. For sufficiently small collision cross sections ( σ ~ m ∼ < 0.1 \tilde{\sigma}_{\rm m}\lower 3.01385pt\hbox{$\;\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\sim}\limits^{<}}\;$}0.1 ), the early stages of core collapse take place in the LMFP regime in which the Knudsen number of the core remains above unity. During this stage, the density and effective temperature of the core increase super-exponentially. With our revised conductivity calibration, we find the time-scale for this catastropic core collapse phase to be t cc = 380 ​ t 0 t_{\rm cc}=380\,t_{0} , roughly 16 percent shorter than the value advocated in previous studies ( Pollack et al., 2015 ; Essig et al., 2019 ; Jiang et al., 2026 , ∼ 455 ​ t 0 \sim 455\,t_{0} ; see e.g.,) . Numerous studies in recent years have assumed that this catastropic collapse continues all the way to the point at which the core becomes relativistic and collapses directly, via a radial instability, to a black hole. However, this is incorrect. As first pointed out in Balberg et al. (2002) , it is unavoidable for the core to become optically thick before it becomes relativistic. The evolution of the core during this SMFP regime is very different from that in the LMFP regime. As the core transitions from the LMFP to the SMFP regime, the mean free path in the core becomes smaller than the core radius, and the core can only transfer heat to the outskirts from its outer layers, rather than from its entire volume. This drastically slows the rate at which the core density and temperature evolve. In addition, a core-within-a-core structure develops, with the inner core continuing to undergo core collapse transferring its heat to the outer core, which expands and slowly transfers the heat to the halo outskirts. Following the gravothermal evolution during these later stages of core collapse is extremely challenging. Standard N N -body simulations can barely follow the evolution of the core past the point where the core density reaches ρ c ≃ 10 3 ​ ρ s \rho_{\rm c}\simeq 10^{3}\rho_{\rm s} , as the time steps required become too small. The SphDSMC code developed here can follow the collapse significantly further, to core densities that are several orders of magnitude larger. However, because of its finite spatial resolution (set by the number of particles used), at some point it becomes impossible to resolve the ever-shrinking mean-free path in the collapsing core. Failure to resolve λ mfp \lambda_{\rm mfp} causes artificially enhanced heat transfer, which in turn causes core collapse to proceed too rapidly. Indeed, we find that the SphDSMC results start to deviate from those obtained using the GTF code once the mean-free path is no longer resolved across the entire core. Unfortunately, GTF codes also face challenges in resolving the core collapse deep into the SMFP regime. In particular, because they are inherently one-dimensional, they fail to account for the development of strong radial anisotropy just outside of the (inner) core. As pointed out in Gurian and May (2025) , such anisotropy can give rise to viscous heat transport. Since this is not taken into account in the GTF codes, the latter may underestimate the rate of heat transfer, causing core collapse to proceed too slowly. Currently, it is unclear whether the discrepancy between the GTF and SphDSMC results in the SMFP regime (depicted in Figs. 8 and 9 ) indicates a failure of the former, the latter, or both. Until this conundrum is resolved, the detailed gravothermal evolution deep into the SMFP regime remains unclear (see also Tokayer & van den Bosch, in prep.). Despite these shortcomings, we have used the GTF code to follow the core collapse of NFW haloes all the way to core densities of ρ c = 10 18 ​ ρ s \rho_{\rm c}=10^{18}\rho_{\rm s} . We used these results to construct an easy-to-use fitting function that describes the core collapse of NFW haloes (as inferred from the gravothermal fluid equations). Taking these results at face value, two important points can be made. First, the time t n t_{n} for the core to collapse to a density ρ c = 10 n ​ ρ s \rho_{\rm c}=10^{n}\rho_{\rm s} does not decline monotonically with σ m \sigma_{\rm m} . Rather, it transitions from t n ∝ σ m − 1 t_{n}\propto\sigma^{-1}_{\rm m} for small cross sections to t n ∝ σ m p t_{n}\propto\sigma^{p}_{\rm m} with p ∼ 1 p\sim 1 for large cross sections. The cross section for which t n ​ ( σ m ) t_{n}(\sigma_{\rm m}) is minimal decreases with increasing n n . Secondly, previous estimates for the formation time t BH t_{\rm BH} of a seed black hole through the gravothermal core collapse of a SIDM halo have been drastically underestimated. In particular, it is typically assumed that t BH = t cc ≃ 455 ​ t 0 t_{\rm BH}=t_{\rm cc}\simeq 455t_{0} ( Pollack et al., 2015 ; Choquette et al., 2019 ; Shah and Adhikari, 2024 ; Roberts et al., 2025a ; Roberts et al., 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ) . However, this is only valid in the LMFP regime and ignores that any core must, at some point, become optically thick before becoming relativistic, which slows down subsequent evolution ( Balberg et al., 2002 ; Gad-Nasr et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2026 , see e.g.,) . In addition, it incorrectly assumes that t BH ∝ σ m − 1 t_{\rm BH}\propto\sigma^{-1}_{\rm m} , and can thus be made arbitrarily small by simply adopting a sufficiently large collision cross section. Based on the (admittedly crude) results presented here, we instead argue that forming seed BHs through the gravothermal collapse of a SIDM halo takes too long for this process to be a viable explanation for the alledged population of supermassive black holes at high redshifts discovered with JWST. Although core collapse can be accelerated by invoking a variety of baryonic processes ( Elbert et al., 2018 ; Sameie et al., 2018 ; Feng et al., 2021 ; Zhong et al., 2023 ) , it is unlikely that this is sufficient to overcome the bottleneck associated with collapse in the SMFP regime.

sections.heading: Appendix A N-body simulations of self-interacting dark matter
sections.text: To account for DM self-interactions in N N -body simulations, we closely follow Vogelsberger et al. (2012, hereafter V+12) . We assume that a particle i i can only scatter with one of its k = 32 k=32 nearest neighbours and compute the expectation value for the number of scattering events of particle i i in time step Δ ​ t \Delta t according to ⟨ N scat , i ⟩ = 1 2 ​ ∑ j σ m ​ m p ​ W ​ ( r i ​ j , h i ) ​ | 𝐯 j − 𝐯 i | ​ Δ ​ t . \langle N_{{\rm scat},i}\rangle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j}\sigma_{m}\,m_{\rm p}\,W(r_{ij},h_{i})\,|{\bf v}_{j}-{\bf v}_{i}|\,\Delta t\,. (A.1) Here, the summation is over the k k nearest neighbours, m p m_{\rm p} is the particle mass, W ⁡ ( r , h ) W(r,h) is a kernel function that describes the ‘extent’ of the simulation particle in configuration space, and h i h_{i} is the distance enclosing the k k nearest neighbours of particle i i . The factor 1 / 2 1/2 is needed to avoid double counting. The actual number of interactions for particle i i is drawn from a Poisson distribution with an expectation value equal to ⟨ N scat , i ⟩ \langle N_{{\rm scat},i}\rangle . As detailed below, this is where our approach differs from that of V+12 and many others. Figure A.1: Results of Monte-Carlo simulations in which each of 5 × 10 6 5\times 10^{6} particles, all with the same initial velocity v init = 3 ​ σ v_{\rm init}=3\sigma , are scattered against random particles from a heat bath of constant temperature T = 3 ​ σ T=\sqrt{3}\sigma . Each particle is integrated for a total duration of Δ ​ T \Delta T , using N step N_{\rm step} time steps of Δ ​ t = Δ ​ T / N step \Delta t=\Delta T/N_{\rm step} . Each time step Δ ​ t \Delta t the expectation value for the number of scatter events in the subsequent Δ ​ t \Delta t is updated based on the particle’s new velocity using equations ( A.8 ) and ( A.9 ). Different columns correspond to different N step N_{\rm step} , ranging from 2048 2048 in the left-most panel to 1 1 in the right-most panel. Larger values of N step N_{\rm step} correspond to a smaller effective value for ζ \zeta , as indicated. Top Panels: Coloured histograms show the distributions of v P / σ v_{\rm P}/\sigma after a time Δ ​ T \Delta T , while the grey-shaded histograms show the MB velocity distribution of the heat bath. The sharp peak at v / σ = 3 v/\sigma=3 corresponds to the particles that did not experience any scattering event during the entire time interval Δ ​ T \Delta T . Bottom Panels: The (normalised) distributions of N scat N_{\rm scat} , the number of scattering events particle P P experienced per time step Δ ​ t \Delta t . Despite large differences in the latter, the PDFs of the final velocities for P P are virtually indistinguishable. This justifies the use of multiple scattering events per time step. We impose the following constraint on the time step Δ ​ t < ( Δ ​ t ) SI ≡ ζ max ⁡ ( 1 2 ​ ρ i ​ σ m ​ ⟨ v rel ⟩ i ) . \Delta t<(\Delta t)_{\rm SI}\equiv\frac{\zeta}{{\rm max}(\frac{1}{2}\,\rho_{i}\,\sigma_{\rm m}\,\langle v_{\rm rel}\rangle_{i})}\,. (A.2) Here, ζ \zeta is a free parameter, ρ i = m p ​ ∑ j W ⁡ ( r i ​ j , h i ) \rho_{i}=m_{\rm p}\sum_{j}W(r_{ij},h_{i}) , ⟨ v rel ⟩ i = 1 k ​ ∑ j | 𝐯 j − 𝐯 i | \langle v_{\rm rel}\rangle_{i}={1\over k}\sum_{j}|{\bf v}_{j}-{\bf v}_{i}| where the sum is over the k k nearest neighbours of particle i i , and the maximum in the denominator is taken over all N N simulation particles i i . It is common to pick a value for ζ \zeta such that the probability of a particle to scatter more than once per time step is negligible. For example, V+12 use ζ ∼ 0.01 \zeta\sim 0.01 , while others have advocated even smaller values ( Vogelsberger et al., 2019 ; Mace et al., 2024 ; Palubski et al., 2024 ) . Our approach is different. We set ζ = 0.5 \zeta=0.5 and allow multiple scattering events per particle per time step. In particular, once it has been determined that a target particle i i has N scat ≥ 1 N_{\rm scat}\geq 1 scattering events in time step Δ ​ t \Delta t , we proceed as follows. For each scattering event particle i i is scattered against one of its k k nearest neighbours, where the probability to scatter with particle j j is given by P i ​ j = W ⁡ ( r i ​ j , h i ) ​ | 𝐯 j − 𝐯 i | ∑ j W ⁡ ( r i ​ j , h i ) ​ | 𝐯 j − 𝐯 i | , P_{ij}=\frac{W(r_{ij},h_{i})\,|{\bf v}_{j}-{\bf v}_{i}|}{\sum_{j}W(r_{ij},h_{i})\,|{\bf v}_{j}-{\bf v}_{i}|}\,, (A.3) Once a particle j j is selected for a collision with i i , we update their velocities following the same procedure as for the SphDSMC code (see Section 2.2 ). sections.heading: A.1 Multiple Scattering
sections.text: The key difference between our approach and that of V+12 is that we interpret the rhs of equation ( A.1 ) as an expectation value for the number of scatter events, while V+12 interpret it as the probability P 1 P_{1} that the particle in question scatters once, and only once, in time step Δ ​ t \Delta t . Given that the formal expression for P 1 P_{1} is given by P 1 = ⟨ N scat ⟩ ​ exp − ⟨ N scat ⟩ P_{1}=\langle N_{\rm scat}\rangle\,\exp^{-\langle N_{\rm scat}\rangle} (A.7) we see that the two approaches become effectively equal in the limit where P 1 P_{1} is very small. This in turn requires a sufficiently small time step, and thus a small value for ζ \zeta . To our knowledge, all numerical simulations of SIDM to date have adopted the same approach as V+12, to which we refer as the ‘standard method’ in what follows. It is based on the notion that one should not allow a particle to scatter more than once per timestep. The motivation for this restriction is that once a particle has scattered, its velocity changes, which impacts its subsequent scatter probability. However, as we demonstrate below, allowing multiple scattering events per particle per time step is not a concern (within limits), as long as one properly interprets the rhs of equation ( A.1 ) as an expectation value. This means that one can allow values for ζ \zeta that are actually much larger than the small values usually adopted in the standard model, which can drastically speed up the simulation especially during the core collapse phase. In order to probe the impact of multi-scattering per time step, we perform a simple idealised experiment. Consider a particle P P of initial velocity v init v_{\rm init} in a sea of particles that follow a Maxwell-Boltmann (MB) velocity distribution with 1D velocity dispersion σ \sigma (i.e., a thermal bath of temperature T = 3 ​ σ T=\sqrt{3}\sigma ). We assume a homogeneous density of arbitrary value and a collisional cross section per unit mass, also of arbitrary value, and pick a time step Δ ​ t \Delta t such that ⟨ N scat ⟩ = 0.001 × 2 n \langle N_{\rm scat}\rangle=0.001\times 2^{n} . Here, n = 0 , 1 , 2 , … , 11 n=0,1,2,...,11 is the one free parameter of our experiment and ⟨ N scat ⟩ = 0.5 ​ σ m ​ ρ ​ ⟨ v rel ⟩ ​ Δ ​ t . \langle N_{\rm scat}\rangle=0.5\,\sigma_{\rm m}\,\rho\,\langle v_{\rm rel}\rangle\,\Delta t\,. (A.8) The expectation value for the relative velocity of P P with respect to a random particle drawn from the MB distribution is analytical and given by ⟨ v rel ⟩ = σ ⁡ [ 2 π ​ exp ⁡ ( − x 2 2 ) + ( x + 1 x ) ​ erf ​ ( x 2 ) ] , \langle v_{\rm rel}\rangle=\sigma\left[\sqrt{2\over\pi}\exp\left(-{x^{2}\over 2}\right)+\left(x+{1\over x}\right)\,{\rm erf}\left({x\over\sqrt{2}}\right)\right]\,, (A.9) where x = v P / σ x=v_{\rm P}/\sigma . For each value of n n , we ‘evolve’ P P for a total integration time of Δ ​ T = N step ​ Δ ​ t \Delta T=N_{\rm step}\,\Delta t where N step = 2 11 − n N^{\rm step}=2^{11-n} . Note that this leaves Δ ​ T \Delta T invariant among all experiments (i.e., for all n n ). Larger values of n n implies fewer, but longer time steps Δ ​ t \Delta t , and a larger expectation value for the number of scatter events per time step. Since ζ \zeta is equal to the maximum value of ⟨ N scat ⟩ \langle N_{\rm scat}\rangle allowed per time step (cf. equation [ A.2 ]), as we increase n n we effectively increase ζ \zeta from 0.001 0.001 ( n = 0 n=0 ) to 2.048 2.048 ( n = 11 n=11 ). Hence, these experiments probe the impact of varying ζ \zeta by more than three orders of magnitude. Figure A.2: Summary statistics of the multi-scatter Monte-Carlo simulations. The top panel plots the ratio ⟨ v P ⟩ n / ⟨ v P ⟩ 0 \langle v_{\rm P}\rangle_{\rm n}/\langle v_{\rm P}\rangle_{0} . Here, ⟨ v P ⟩ \langle v_{\rm P}\rangle is the average velocity of particle P P after a fixed total integration time of Δ ​ T \Delta T and the subscript indicates the value of n = 11 − log 2 ⁡ ( Δ ​ T / Δ ​ t ) n=11-\log_{2}(\Delta T/\Delta t) used in the experiment, with Δ ​ t \Delta t the timestep used per integration step. Different colours correspond to different values for the initial velocity v init v_{\rm init} , as indicated. Results are plotted as a function of the effective value of ζ = 0.001 × 2 n \zeta=0.001\times 2^{n} , which reflects the expectation value for the maximum number of scatter events per time step. The vertical dotted line corresponds to ζ = 0.5 \zeta=0.5 which is the value adopted in our N N -body simulations. The bottom panels plot the ratio Γ n / Γ 0 \Gamma_{\rm n}/\Gamma_{0} of the scatter rates averaged over the period Δ ​ T \Delta T . Errorbars, computed from the variance among ten realisations, are smaller than the symbols shown. Each time step Δ ​ t \Delta t we proceed as in our N N -body code: we draw a number of scattering events N scat N_{\rm scat} from a Poisson distribution with a mean of ⟨ N scat ⟩ \langle N_{\rm scat}\rangle , and scatter particle P P a total of N scat N_{\rm scat} times against particles drawn at random from the MB distribution, each time updating the velocity of P P . Each subsequent time step, we recompute ⟨ N scat ⟩ \langle N_{\rm scat}\rangle using the updated value for v P v_{\rm P} , which enters in the calculation of ⟨ v rel ⟩ \langle v_{\rm rel}\rangle . At the end of the N step N_{\rm step} time steps, we register the final velocity of P P as well as the total number of scatter events it experienced. Note that Δ ​ t \Delta t is based on the value of ⟨ N scat ⟩ \langle N_{\rm scat}\rangle at the initial time step, when v P = v init v_{\rm P}=v_{\rm init} . It is then kept fixed during the entire period Δ ​ T \Delta T . For each value of n n , we repeat this experiment a total of 5 × 10 6 5\times 10^{6} times, each time starting P P with the same v init v_{\rm init} . The blue histogram in the top-left panel of Fig. A.1 shows the resulting distribution of v P v_{\rm P} for n = 0 n=0 and v init = 3 ​ σ v_{\rm init}=3\sigma . The grey-shaded histogram shows the MB distribution of the heat bath and is shown for comparison. Note the large spike at v P = v init = 3 ​ σ v_{\rm P}=v_{\rm init}=3\sigma , which represents all realisations in which P P did not scatter throughout the entire period Δ ​ T \Delta T . The blue histogram in the bottom-left panel shows the distribution of N scat N_{\rm scat} , the number of scatter events per small time step Δ ​ t \Delta t , in all 5 × 10 6 5\times 10^{6} realisations. Since for n = 0 n=0 the time step Δ ​ t \Delta t is tuned so that the initial ⟨ N scat ⟩ = 0.001 \langle N_{\rm scat}\rangle=0.001 , the vast majority of time steps have N scat = 0 N_{\rm scat}=0 or 1 1 ; the fraction of time steps with N scat ≥ 2 N_{\rm scat}\geq 2 is only 2.4 × 10 − 6 2.4\times 10^{-6} . The average number of scatter events experienced by P P per time step Δ ​ t \Delta t is 0.00088 0.00088 , which is somewhat smaller than the initial expectation value of 0.001 0.001 . The reason for this difference is that as P P thermalizes, its average velocity approaches that of the MB distribution, which is smaller than v init v_{\rm init} . Hence, as P P thermalizes, ⟨ v rel ⟩ \langle v_{\rm rel}\rangle decreases, which reduces its probability of scattering. The orange, violet and ocre histograms in Fig. A.1 show the results for n = 6 n=6 , 9 9 and 11 11 , corresponding to N step = 64 N_{\rm step}=64 , 4 4 and 1 1 , respectively. Recall that in each case P P is integrated for the same total duration Δ ​ T \Delta T , but that the time step used, and thus the effective value of ζ \zeta , increases with n n as indicated in each panel. Note that the distributions of the final velocities (top panels) are virtually indistinguishable from those for n = 0 n=0 . Yet, the lower panels show that the corresponding distributions for N scat N_{\rm scat} , the number of scatter events per time step Δ ​ t \Delta t , are very different, with averages of ⟨ N scat ⟩ = 0.028 \langle N_{\rm scat}\rangle=0.028 , 0.465 0.465 , and 2.047 2.047 , respectively. However, the average number of scatter events experienced over the entire time interval Δ ​ T \Delta T remains fairly similar; it slightly increases from 1.802 1.802 in the case of n = 0 n=0 to 2.047 2.047 in the case where n = 11 n=11 . This is a consequence of the fact that when Δ ​ t \Delta t is too large, the scattering probabilities are not properly updated based on the evolving velocity of P P . Hence, advocates of the ‘standard model’ are correct that allowing multi-scattering per particle per time step can cause a systematic error in the scatter frequency. However, unless the values for ⟨ N scat ⟩ \langle N_{\rm scat}\rangle per time step are allowed to be excessively large (which we quantify below), the impact of this systematic has a negligible impact. The first hint that this is indeed the case is provided by the top panels of Fig. A.1 , which shows that the PDF for v P v_{\rm P} appears invariant to increasing ⟨ N scat ⟩ \langle N_{\rm scat}\rangle , and thus ζ \zeta , by over three orders of magnitude, from 0.001 0.001 to 2.048 2.048 . Figure A.3: The impact of varying ζ \zeta on N N -body simulations of the gravothermal evolution of the NFWc20 ∗ halo simulated with N p = 10 5 N_{\rm p}=10^{5} particles. Each simulation uses a cross section σ m = 50 ​ cm 2 ​ g − 1 \sigma_{\rm m}=50\>{\rm cm}^{2}\,{\rm g}^{-1} , starts from the same initial conditions, and uses a Plummer softening of ϵ = 0.025 \epsilon=0.025 . Top panel shows the evolution of the core density, middle panel shows the ratio of the scatter rate in the simulation to the expected scatter rate computed using equation ( 24 ), and the bottom panel shows the level of energy conservation. Note that changing ζ \zeta by two orders of magnitude has no significant impact on the simulation results, except for the level of noise in Γ sim / Γ pred \Gamma_{\rm sim}/\Gamma_{\rm pred} , which increases with descreasing ζ \zeta due to the fact that smaller ζ \zeta implies smaller time steps. To better quantify this, the top panel of Fig. A.2 plots the ratio ⟨ v P ⟩ n / ⟨ v P ⟩ 0 \langle v_{\rm P}\rangle_{\rm n}/\langle v_{\rm P}\rangle_{0} , where the subscript indicates the value of n n used in the experiment, as a function of the effective value of ζ = 0.001 × 2 n \zeta=0.001\times 2^{n} . The vertical dotted line corresponds to ζ = 0.5 \zeta=0.5 , which is the value we have adopted in our simulations. Different colours correspond to different values for the initial velocity v init v_{\rm init} , as indicated. As is evident, ⟨ v P ⟩ \langle v_{\rm P}\rangle is extremely robust to changes in ζ \zeta , and we have verified that this also holds for the 5, 50 and 95 percentiles of the full v P v_{\rm P} distributions. The bottom panels plot the ratio Γ n / Γ 0 \Gamma_{\rm n}/\Gamma_{0} of the scattering rates, averaged over the period Δ ​ T \Delta T . Note that Γ n \Gamma_{\rm n} converges to a constant value when ζ \zeta is sufficiently small. However, when ζ \zeta is too large it causes an over(under)-estimate of the scattering rate for particles that are moving faster (slower) than the average. Note, though, that the results shown here are for particle beams of a single initial velocity. When averaged over an entire distribution of particle velocities, the error in the total scattering rate will be significantly smaller. In addition, in the N N -body simulations ζ \zeta reflects the expectation value for the maximum number of scattering events per time step, whereas in the idealised experiment above we have assumed that all particles have the same ⟨ N scat ⟩ \langle N_{\rm scat}\rangle . Finally, to explicitly demonstrate that large values of ζ \zeta are not detrimental to the simulation outcome, we have run the NFWc20 ∗ halo using different values of ζ \zeta . Fig. A.3 shows the evolution of the central density of our NFWc20 ∗ halo with a collisional cross section of σ ~ m = 0.375 \tilde{\sigma}_{\rm m}=0.375 , run with various values of ζ \zeta , as indicated. Note that here we have used simulations with N = 10 5 N=10^{5} particles only, as runs with small ζ \zeta take extremely long to complete (the ζ = 0.1 \zeta=0.1 run took 244 244 hours on a single processor, compared to 34 34 hours for our fiducial value of ζ = 0.5 \zeta=0.5 ). The top panel shows the evolution of the central density, which shows almost no dependence on ζ \zeta . The middle panel shows the ratio of the scattering rate in the simulation, Γ sim \Gamma_{\rm sim} , to the predicted scattering rate based on the instantaneous density and velocity dispersion profile (see Section 3.1 ). Within the noise, this ratio is consistent with unity at all times and for all values of ζ \zeta probed. Note that Γ sim \Gamma_{\rm sim} is inferred from the number of scattering events integrated over a period of ten simulation time steps. Since smaller values of ζ \zeta imply smaller time steps, the Poisson noise increases with decreasing ζ \zeta . The bottom panel plots the evolution of | Δ ​ E / E 0 | = | [ E ⁡ ( t ) − E ⁡ ( 0 ) ] / E ⁡ ( 0 ) | |\Delta E/E_{0}|=|[E(t)-E(0)]/E(0)| where E ⁡ ( t ) E(t) is the total energy of the system at time t t . Note that energy conservation is typically at the level of 10 − 4 10^{-4} , again independent of the value of ζ \zeta .

sections.heading: Appendix B Realisation Noise
sections.text: Figure B.1: The impact of mass resolution on modelling core collapse with the SphDSMC code. From left to right, different panels show results for different N p N_{\rm p} ranging from 10 4 10^{4} (left) to 10 6 10^{6} (right). Each panel shows the results for 7 different simulations of the same NFWc20 ∗ halo using σ m = 25 ​ cm 2 ​ g − 1 \sigma_{\rm m}=25\>{\rm cm}^{2}\,{\rm g}^{-1} ( σ ~ m = 0.19 \tilde{\sigma}_{\rm m}=0.19 ). In the top panels, each simulation starts from a different IC file, while the bottom panels use an identical IC file, but a different seed for the random number generator used to model particle scattering. Black, dashed curves show the prediction from the GTF code using ( α , β ) = ( 0.50 , 0.90 ) (\alpha,\beta)=(0.50,0.90) and are shown for comparison. Each simulation of core collapse, be it with the SphDSMC code or with an N N -body code, is subject to two sources of realisation noise. The first arises from the specific initial conditions that are set up by sampling particles from the system’s distribution function as described in Section 2.4 . The second comes from the scattering process, which requires drawing several random numbers to decide which pairs of particles are going to scatter and to pick a random scattering angle for those that do. Here we investigate the impact of both sources of realisation noise. We construct a suite of random realisations of ICs for the NFWc20 ∗ halo (see Table 1). We consider three different mass resolutions: N p = 10 4 N_{\rm p}=10^{4} , 10 5 10^{5} and 10 6 10^{6} , and for each of these we construct 7 different realisations using different random seeds. We run each of these 24 simulations with the SphDSMC code, always with the same numerical parameters and with a collision cross section σ m = 25 ​ cm 2 ​ g − 1 \sigma_{\rm m}=25\>{\rm cm}^{2}\,{\rm g}^{-1} ( σ ~ m = 0.19 \tilde{\sigma}_{\rm m}=0.19 ). The results are shown in the upper panels of Fig. B.1 . Different panels correspond to different mass resolutions, while different colours correspond to different IC realisations. The black dashed curves show the prediction from the GTF code using ( α , β ) = ( 0.50 , 0.90 ) (\alpha,\beta)=(0.50,0.90) and are shown for comparison. For N p ∼ > 10 6 N_{\rm p}\lower 3.01385pt\hbox{$\;\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\sim}\limits^{>}}\;$}10^{6} the impact of realisation noise is modest at best, resulting in a ∼ 2 \sim 2 percent standard deviation in the collapse time. This is small enough for an accurate calibration of the GTF conductivity parameters α \alpha and β \beta . However, for N p ≤ 10 5 N_{\rm p}\leq 10^{5} realisation noise causes a large divergence in collapse times, ranging from core collapse that is too early to cases where core collapse is drastically delayed. These findings are in excellent agreement with Mace et al. (2024) , who found very similar behaviour for N N -body simulations. In the bottom panels, the ICs of all simulations are identical, but different random seeds are used to sample the scattering events. As is evident, this results in a significantly reduced level of stochastisticity, indicating that the realisation noise that arises from the ICs is the dominant source of stochasticity.

Box 208120, New Haven, CT 06520-8120 Abstract Self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) haloes undergo gravothermal evolution whose late-time behaviour is central to predictions for dense substructure and black-hole seed formation. We revisit the calibration of this evolution using a new spherical Direct Simulation Monte Carlo code, SphDSMC , which follows spherically symmetric SIDM systems without force softening and to substantially higher central densities than standard N N -body simulations. We compare SphDSMC calculations with conventional N N -body simulations and with one-dimensional gravothermal fluid models. We show that N N -body results converge to SphDSMC only for softening lengths significantly smaller than those normally adopted for collisionless simulations, and that allowing multiple scatterings per particle per time step does not introduce significant errors when implemented appropriately. Calibrating the gravothermal fluid equations against SphDSMC , we find that the commonly used harmonic interpolation between the long- and short-mean-free-path conductivities is inaccurate. A gentler transition, however, yields excellent agreement for NFW haloes over a range of concentrations and truncation radii, with a single long-mean-free-path conductivity parameter. The revised calibration gives a long-mean-free-path collapse time that is somewhat shorter than previous estimates, but we show that collapse slows dramatically once the core becomes optically thick. We provide fitting functions for the late-time evolution and argue that black-hole seed formation by SIDM gravothermal collapse has generally been underestimated in duration, making it unlikely to explain the massive high-redshift black holes inferred from JWST observations without additional physics. Keywords: Dark Matter – Gravitational Instability – Galaxy Nuclei – Galaxy Dark Matter Haloes – N-body simulations 1 Introduction Self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) remains one of the most widely studied alternatives to collisionless cold dark matter (CDM). In SIDM models, dark-matter particles undergo non-gravitational scattering, allowing heat and momentum transport within haloes while preserving the large-scale phenomenology of Λ \Lambda CDM ( Spergel and Steinhardt, 2000 ; Tulin and Yu, 2018 ; Adhikari et al., 2025 ) . Self-scattering initially transports heat from the hotter outer halo into the colder inner region, driving the formation of an approximately isothermal core and reducing the central density. At later times, the direction of net heat flow reverses and the system enters a gravothermal-collapse phase, during which the central region contracts, heats up and becomes denser ( Lynden-Bell and Wood, 1968 ; Balberg et al., 2002 ; Koda and Shapiro, 2011 ; Outmezguine et al., 2023 ) . This behaviour is closely related to the gravothermal catastrophe long studied in collisional stellar systems. Gravothermal collapse has attracted increasing attention because it provides a natural mechanism for generating substantial halo-to-halo diversity. Haloes with similar virial masses but different concentrations, accretion histories or tidal environments need not be observed in the same thermodynamic state: some may still be in the core-expansion phase, while others may already have collapsed to much higher central densities. This offers a plausible route to understanding the observed diversity of rotation curves, including the coexistence of diffuse and comparatively dense systems within the same broad mass range ( Ren et al., 2019 ; Sameie et al., 2020 ; Nadler et al., 2023 ; Roberts et al., 2025b ; Fischer and Yu, 2026 ) . Related considerations arise in the context of strong gravitational lensing. Observational studies have pointed to unexpectedly dense perturbers ( Minor et al., 2021 ) and to an excess of galaxy-galaxy strong lensing in clusters relative to standard theoretical expectations ( Meneghetti et al., 2023 ; Natarajan et al., 2026 ) . SIDM subhaloes that have undergone gravothermal collapse provide a natural source of compact, high-density structures capable of enhancing such signals, particularly when tidal effects accelerate their evolution after infall ( Nishikawa et al., 2020 ; Gilman et al., 2021 ; Zeng et al., 2022 ; Shah and Adhikari, 2024 ; Dutra et al., 2025 ) . Perhaps the most far-reaching implication of SIDM gravothermal collapse is that sufficiently deep collapse can trigger black hole (BH) formation. In particular, if the self-interactions of the dark matter particles do not allow the formation of any bound states, the runaway gravothermal collapse will drive the core to relativistic velocities at which point the core undergoes catastrophic collapse into a BH via the radial instability ( Zel’dovich and Podurets, 1966 ; Shapiro and Teukolsky, 1985 ; Balberg and Shapiro, 2002 ) . More recent studies have revived this idea in several contexts, including intermediate-mass BH formation in Milky Way satellites ( Meshveliani et al., 2023 ) , and BH seeding in high-redshift haloes which might help to explain the unexpectedly early appearance of massive accreting BHs in the Universe ( Pollack et al., 2015 ; Choquette et al., 2019 ; Feng et al., 2021 ; Feng et al., 2022 ) . This connection has become especially timely in light of the discovery by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) of the “little red dots” (LRDs): a numerous population of compact, red, broad-line sources at high redshift that appear consistent with rapidly growing black holes embedded in dense gaseous environments ( Kocevski et al., 2023 ; Greene et al., 2024 ; Matthee et al., 2024 ) . Several recent works have therefore proposed SIDM core collapse as a viable channel for producing the heavy black-hole seeds needed for LRDs ( Feng et al., 2025 ; Roberts et al., 2026 ; Shen et al., 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ) . In each of these applications, the relevant phenomenology depends sensitively on the gravothermal-collapse time. Whether one is interested in the diversity of dwarf-galaxy rotation curves, the existence of dense strong-lensing perturbers, or the formation of early black-hole seeds, the viability of the SIDM interpretation depends on whether collapse can occur within the available cosmic time. In practice, collapse times are inferred using two main approaches: particle-based N N -body simulations with stochastic scattering and one-dimensional (1D) gravothermal fluid (GTF) calculations. These methods are complementary, but they rely on different assumptions and each has its own shortcomings. The gravothermal fluid approach, introduced for SIDM haloes by Balberg et al. (2002) and developed further in many later studies ( Ahn and Shapiro, 2005 ; Koda and Shapiro, 2011 ; Pollack et al., 2015 ; Essig et al., 2019 ; Nishikawa et al., 2020 ; Outmezguine et al., 2023 ) , assumes a spherical, non-rotating halo evolving quasi-statically through a sequence of hydrostatic states. Its main advantage is that it is inexpensive and can follow the system over a large dynamic range, making it well suited for mapping collapse times across parameter space. The key limitation, however, is that one of the main ingredients, the effective conductivity in the long-mean-free path (LMFP) regime, is not know from first principles. Instead, it is typically parameterised by a single free parameter which is calibrated against the results from N N -body simulations. In addition, one generally interpolates between the long and short-mean-free part (SMFP) regimes using an ad-hoc interpolation scheme that has not been adequately tested. The alternative route is direct N N -body simulation, in which SIDM scattering is implemented probabilistically between neighbouring particles on top of the collisionless gravitational evolution ( Burkert, 2000 ; Kochanek and White, 2000 ; Yoshida et al., 2000 ; Davé et al., 2001 ; Vogelsberger et al., 2012 ; Rocha et al., 2013 ) . The major advantage of this approach is that it does not impose spherical symmetry, hydrostatic equilibrium or isotropy, and can naturally capture mergers, cosmological accretion and tidal stripping ( Vogelsberger et al., 2012 ; Rocha et al., 2013 ; Zavala et al., 2013 ; Sameie et al., 2020 ; Turner et al., 2021 ; Zeng et al., 2022 ) . This is relevant because the collapse time can be strongly altered by the environment: tidal stripping tends to accelerate collapse by steepening the outer density profile and enhancing the outward heat flux ( Nishikawa et al., 2020 ; Sameie et al., 2020 ; Zeng et al., 2022 ; Shah and Adhikari, 2024 ) , while continued accretion, mergers or other heating processes can delay or interrupt collapse ( Ahn and Shapiro, 2005 ; Turner et al., 2021 ; Outmezguine et al., 2023 ; Silverman et al., 2026 ) . On the other hand, properly resolving the gravothermal collapse is numerically challenging. As the core contracts, the central density rises rapidly, local scattering and dynamical time-scales become very short, and the inferred collapse time becomes sensitive to particle number, force softening, time integration, and the details of the scattering implementation ( Meskhidze et al., 2022 ; Palubski et al., 2024 ; Fischer et al., 2024 ; Fischer et al., 2025 ; Mace et al., 2024 ) . Recent numerical studies have shown that these effects can shift the collapse time appreciably, so even the simulation-based estimates are not yet fully settled. This in turn impacts the calibration of the LMFP conductivity used in the GTF codes, and thus the collapse times that these codes predict. In this work we study the gravothermal core collapse of SIDM haloes using a two-step approach. We first present a new simulation code, similar in spirit to the kinetic solver KiSS-SIDM recently developed by Gurian and May (2025) and to the NSphere code developed independently by Kamionkowski and Sigurdson (2026) . This code has several advantages over standard N N -body codes. Here, we use it to calibrate the conductivity used in GTF codes. We show that the harmonic form that has hitherto been used to interpolate the conductivity parameter between the long- and short-mean-free paths is inaccurate. We propose an alternative form and show that a single value for the conductivity parameter in the LMFP regime suffices to model the gravothermal evolution of any NFW halo, independent of its concentration parameter or the level to which it has been truncated. This paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the various numerical methods used here to study the gravothermal evolution of SIDM haloes, including a detailed description of the haloes used throughout. Section 3 starts with a validation of our new SphDSMC code against N N -body simulations, followed by an improved calibration of the conductivity used in the gravothermal fluid equations and a discussion of outstanding issues. In Section 4 we present a detailed discussion of the core collapse time of NFW haloes and present a fitting function that accurately captures the late stages of their gravothermal collapse. This is used in Section 4.1 to demonstrate that the time-scale on which core collapse can produce a seed black hole mass is orders of magnitude larger than previously assumed. We summarize our findings in Section 5 . Finally, Appendix A describes the Monte-Carlo method used in our N N -body simulations, including a detailed demonstration that, contrary to claims in the literature, it is justified to allow multiple scatter events per particle per time. Appendix B discusses the impact of stochasticity due to realisation noise on the ability to determine the core collapse time of an SIDM halo, and Appendix C presents a validation of the new SphDSMC code. Throughout, we assume a flat Λ \Lambda CDM cosmology with Ω m = 0.3 \Omega_{\rm m}=0.3 and H 0 = 70 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=70\>{\rm km}\,{\rm s}^{-1}\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1} , unless stated otherwise. 2 Methodology The main goal of this paper is to use simulations of SIDM haloes undergoing core collapse to calibrate the conductivity used in gravothermal fluid (hereafter GTF ) codes to model the same process. For the simulations, we use a new spherical Direct Simulation Monte Carlo code developed by the authors, called SphDSMC , which is similar to, but independent of, two separate codes recently developed by Gurian and May (2025) and by Kamionkowski and Sigurdson (2026) and Kamionkowski et al. (2026) , respectively. SphDSMC assumes spherical symmetry and integrates the radial coordinates of particles in an N N -body system following the approach pioneered by Hénon and Spitzer more than half a century ago ( Hénon, 1964 ; Hénon, 1971 ; Spitzer and Hart, 1971 ) , while treating the collisional scattering using the Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method ( Bird, 1994 ) . The main advantages of this method are that it (i) is much faster than the N N -body method, (ii) can integrate the system down to much higher core densities, (iii) does not require any particle softening, and (iv) typically results in much better energy conservation than standard N N -body codes. The downside is that it only works for spherically symmetric systems. As already advocated by Gurian and May (2025) and Kamionkowski et al. (2026) this method is ideally suited for studying the core collapse of (spherical) SIDM haloes. The GTF method solves the evolution of a spherical SIDM halo on a 1D radial grid treating the system as a gravothermal fluid following Lynden-Bell and Eggleton (1980) and Balberg et al. (2002) . The main advantages of this method are that it is even faster than the SphDSMC method, and that it is not subject to realisation noise; as input it takes a discretised version of the smooth density and velocity dispersion profiles of the system in question, rather than the phase-space coordinates of a discrete set of points sampled from the system’s distribution function. As shown in Appendix B , suppressing the realisation noise sufficiently for a reliable measure of the core collapse time-scale, N N -body and SphDSMC simulations typically require at least 10 6 10^{6} particles per halo ( Mace et al., 2024 , see also) . As a consequence, it typically takes several hours to simulate the core collapse of a single halo with the SphDSMC code, and 5-10 times longer with a standard N N -body code. The GTF code, on the other hand, typically already yields converged results for a radial grid consisting of only a few hundred bins and it only takes a few seconds to run it to central densities comparable to what can be achieved with SphDSMC or N N -body simulations. The main downside of the GTF method is that it has a free parameter that characterises the conductivity in the LMFP regime. This parameter directly impacts the time-scale on which the system undergoes core collapse but has thus far eluded a derivation from first principles. Hence, it is common to calibrate this parameter against N N -body simulations. However, since the latter are subject to significant uncertainties and systematics (see Palubski et al., 2024 ; Fischer et al., 2024 ; Mace et al., 2024 , and Section 3.1 ) , this gives rise to a catch-22 situation. Indeed, different studies have inferred calibration constants that differ by more than 25% and it is currently unclear whether this reflects inconsistencies among the N N -body simulations or whether the calibration parameter itself varies with properties of the halo in question. The goal of this paper is to avoid these issues by calibrating the GTF method against results of the SphDSMC method. As we will show, part of the issue is that the ad-hoc interpolation scheme that has been used to link the short- and long-mean-free path regimes is inaccurate.
